title: Mr. X & The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission
text:
Decision
Mr. X & The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission
From
Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC)
Case number: OIC-162236-Q9X0T0
Published on 10 July 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Preliminary Matters
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Right of Appeal
Whether the Commission was justified, under sections 29(1), 30(1), 35(1), 36(1) and 37(1) of the FOI Act, in refusing access to records relating to its review of a merger involving two named private companies
10 July 2026
Background
In an FOI request dated 8 April 2025, the applicant sought access to records relating to the Commission’s review of a merger involving two named private companies. In particular, the request sought access to relevant submissions, requests from the Commission for further information and responses to same, and records of interviews carried out by the Commission. In the course of subsequent correspondence exchanged between the parties, the Commission advised the applicant that his request was likely to involve a voluminous amount of records, and sought to narrow the scope of the request. Thereafter, the applicant refined his request, specifically seeking access to i) any cover letters from participating third parties to include any indices or lists of attachments, ii) any legal reports and iii) any technical reports, relating to the Commission’s review of the merger identified in his original request.
In its decision on the FOI request dated 3 July 2025, the Commission refused the request, citing sections 29(1), 30(1), 35(1), 36(1) and 37(1) of the FOI Act as grounds for its refusal. On 28 July 2025, the applicant sought an internal review from the Commission of its initial decision. In its internal review decision dated 18 August 2025, the Commission affirmed its original decision. On 24 October 2025, the applicant sought a review from this Office of the Commission’s decision on his FOI request.
I have now completed my review in accordance with section 22(2) of the FOI Act. In carrying out my review, I have had regard to the relevant correspondence exchanged between the parties, the submissions made by the applicant in his application for review and the submissions made by the Commission in support of its decision. I have decided to conclude this review by way of a formal, binding decision.
Scope of Review
This review is solely concerned with whether the Commission was justified, under sections 29(1), 30(1), 35(1), 36(1) and 37(1) of the FOI Act, in refusing to grant the applicant access to the records sought.
Preliminary Matters
Before I address the substantive issues arising, I wish to make some preliminary points. First of all, it is important to note that section 22(12)(b) of the FOI Act provides that a decision to refuse to grant a request shall be presumed not to have been justified unless the head of the relevant FOI body shows to the Information Commissioner's satisfaction that its decision was justified. This means that the onus is on the Commission of satisfying this Office that it was entitled to rely on the relevant provisions of the FOI Act in its decision on the applicant’s FOI request.
Secondly, section 25(3) of the FOI Act requires me to take all reasonable precautions in the course of a review to prevent disclosure of information contained in an exempt record. This means that the extent to which I can describe the contents of the record at issue is limited.
It is also relevant to note that the FOI Act places no constraints on the uses to which information released under FOI can subsequently be put. Accordingly, the release of information under FOI is generally regarded as release, at least potentially, to the world at large.
Finally, section 13(4) of the FOI Act requires that, subject to the legislation, any reasons a requester gives for making a request shall be disregarded. This means that this Office cannot have regard to the applicant’s motives for seeking the records in question, except insofar as those motives reflect what might be regarded as public interest factors in favour of release of information, where the FOI Act requires a consideration of public interest.
Analysis and Findings
The records at issue
The Commission identified a total of 275 relevant records, across nine categories. It cited section 35(1) of the FOI Act as a basis to withhold all 275 the records in full, due to the circumstances in which they were provided (i.e. by parties participating in the merger review process). In addition to relying on section 35(1) in respect of each of the records, the Commission applied the remainder of the exemptions on which it relied to withhold the records as follows:
1. Records 1 and 2 are Requests for Information (RFIs) issued by the Commission to the two primary parties involved in the merger during Phase 2 of the merger review process. The Commission relied on sections 29(1), 30(1), 36(1) and 37(1) to withhold both records in full.
2. Records 3 to 59 are responses received by the Commission to the RFIs issued during Phase 2. The Commission relied on sections 36(1) and 37(1) to withhold all of these records in full.
3. Records 60 to 63 are third-party submissions made to the Commission during its Phase 2 investigation process in relation to the merger. The Commission withheld each of these records in full under sections 36(1) and 37(1).
4. Records 64 to 71 are third party submissions made to the Commission during its Phase 1
investigation process in relation to the merger. Again, the Commission withheld each of these records in full under sections 36(1) and 37(1).
5. Record 72 is the Commission’s Phase 2 report on the merger, which it withheld from release in full under sections 29(1), 30(1), 36(1) and 37(1).
6. Records 73 to 90 are notes of interviews conducted by the Commission with third parties in relation to the merger, all of which the Commission again withheld in full under sections 29(1), 30(1), 36(1) and 37(1).
7. Records 91 and 92 are further RFIs issued by the Commission in May 2024 to the two primary parties involved in the merger. Again, the Commission cited sections 29(1), 30(1), 36(1) and 37(1) to fully withhold these two records.
8. Records 93 to 141 comprise the response to the May 2024 RFI from one of the principal parties to merger. The Commission relied on the following provisions of the FOI Act to fully withhold each of these records –
o records 93, 101 to 103, 115, 118, 132 and 139 were withheld under section 36(1);
o records 94, 98 to 100, 112, 114, 116 to 117, 119 to 131, 133 to 138 and 141 were withheld under sections 36(1) and 37(1);
o record 106 was withheld under sections 29(1), 30(1) and 36(1).
9. Records 142 to 275 comprise the response to the May 2024 RFI from the other principal party to the merger. The Commission relied on the following provisions of the FOI Act to withhold each of these records in full –
o records 142 and 150 were withheld under sections 29(1), 30(1), 36(1) and 37(1);
o records 143 to 145, 152, 155, 160 to 167, 169 to 171, 173 to 174, 181, 183 to 184, 187 to 188, 191 to 194, 196 to 198, 201, 207, 209, 212 to 214, 216, 218 to 219, 221 to 227, 229 to 230, 239, 242 to 244, 247 to 255, 258 to 263, 268 and 270 were withheld under sections 36(1) and 37(1);
o records 147 to 149, 151, 153 to 154, 156 to 159, 176 to 180, 182, 185 to 186, 189 to 190, 195, 199 to 200, 202 to 206, 208, 210 to 211, 215, 217, 220, 228, 231, 233 to 234, 236 to 238, 245 to 246, 256 to 257, 264 to 267, 269 and 271 to 275 were withheld under sections and 36(1);
o records 168, 232, 235 and 240 to 241 were withheld under section 37(1).
Section 35(1)
In circumstances where the Commission relied on section 35(1) to withhold in full all of the records at issue, I consider it appropriate to examine the applicability of this provision of the FOI Act first of all. In its submissions, the Commission relied primarily on subsection (a) of section 35(1), while also noting its view that subsection (b) was also applicable. In the circumstances, I consider section 35(1)(a) the most appropriate provision of the FOI Act under which to examine the Commission’s arguments that the records are exempt from release.
Section 35(1)(a) provides for the mandatory refusal of a request where the record sought contains information given to an FOI body in confidence. This provision of the FOI Act contains four requirements, all of which must be satisfied in order for a record to fall within its scope;
• the information must have been given to an FOI body in confidence;
• the information must have been given on the understanding that it would be treated by the FOI body as confidential;
• disclosure of the information would be likely to prejudice the giving to the body of further similar information from the same person or other persons; and
• it is important to the body that such further similar information should continue to be given to the body.
The Commission’s submissions
Section 35(1)(a)
In its submissions, the Commission noted that a key component in evaluating the applicability of section 35(1)(a) is an assessment of the circumstances in which the relevant information was provided and the expectation of confidentiality. It argued that, in this case, the circumstances in which the information in the records was imparted to it, and the expectations of confidentiality on the part of the parties providing the information, clearly engaged section 35(1)(a). The Commission argued that the information in the records had been provided explicitly and implicitly on a confidential basis, in circumstances where there was a clear and mutual understanding that it would be treated as such. It stated that the nature of merger reviews, as set out in its guidance and procedures, requires undertakings to provide full details of a proposed transaction in order to enable a proper assessment to be carried out. According to the Commissions, this necessarily involves the disclosure of information that would not otherwise enter the public domain.
In relation to the four requirements of section 35(1)(a), the Commission submitted that, in the context of merger reviews, all four are clearly met. It stated that its merger review process requires notifying parties to provide comprehensive and highly sensitive information regarding their businesses, including detailed financial and commercial data, forward-looking business strategies, and internal assessments of markets and competitors. It noted that confidential submissions from relevant third parties are also sought during this process. It argued that such information is provided explicitly and implicitly on a confidential basis, in circumstances where there is a clear and mutual understanding that it will be treated as such.
The first and second requirements
The Commission argued that the information at issue was provided to it in the context of a formal merger review process and for the limited purpose of enabling the assessment of the proposed transaction. In such circumstances, according to the Commission, it was reasonable for the relevant parties, including the notifying parties, customers and competitors, to expect that such information would be treated as confidential and not disclosed more widely. The Commission stated that this element of confidentiality underpins the merger review process and it would not be possible for it to perform this function without it. In these circumstances, it argued that the first and second requirements of section 35(1)(a) are satisfied.
The third requirement
The Commission argued that the third requirement is also met, in circumstances where (according to its submissions) disclosure of the records would be likely to prejudice its receipt of further similar information. It argued that if the parties involved in a merger or other related third parties could not rely on the confidentiality of their submissions, they may limit the scope or detail of the information provided, decline to provide commercially sensitive material or be unwilling to engage with it as part of the merger review process. According to the Commission, disclosure of the records at issue would expose, or allow competitors to derive, sensitive commercial information relating to the parties involved, which would in turn undermine the willingness of future parties to provide it with full and candid information. The Commission argued that such an outcome would prejudice the provision of further similar information to it and would have a direct and detrimental impact on its ability to carry out effective merger reviews, which it argued by extension would have a detrimental impact on businesses and consumers.
The fourth requirement
The Commission argued that the fourth requirement in section 35(1)(a) is fundamental in the context of the records under review. It stated that the merger review process is heavily dependent on the voluntary provision of complete, accurate and candid information by notifying parties and third parties, including highly sensitive commercial matters. It stated that the disclosure of sensitive commercial information in the records at issue would deter parties from engaging with it in future. The Commission argued that it is of the utmost importance to it that it continues to be provided with such information on a confidential basis and argued that, without this, it would be unable to properly assess the competitive effects of mergers or to fulfil its statutory mandate. The Commission argued that the importance of confidentiality in this process cannot be overstated, and that such confidentiality underpins the quality and reliability of evidence available to it, as well as the willingness of stakeholders to cooperate and the overall integrity and effectiveness of the merger review process.
The public interest test – section 35(3)
The exemption at section 35(1)(a) of the FOI Act is subject to a public interest test in section 35(3), which provides that subsection (a) of section 35(1) shall not apply in relation to a case in which, in the opinion of the FOI body, the public interest would, on balance, be better served by granting than by refusing to grant the FOI request.
In its submissions on section 35(3), the Commission stated that the balance of the public interest in this case weighs clearly in favour of refusal. It stated that, although there is a recognised public interest in transparency and accountability, this must be balanced against the strong public interest in ensuring the effective enforcement of competition law, maintaining a robust and credible merger review process and protecting the flow of confidential information necessary for regulatory decision-making. The Commission noted the decision of the Supreme Court in Minister for Communications, Energy and Natural Resources v The Information Commissioner & Ors [2020] IESC 57 (“the eNet case”), in which the Court stated that the public interest in favour of disclosure cannot be equated with the general public interest in openness and transparency set out in the FOI Act. Instead, the Court found that the public interest in disclosure must be something more than the general public interest in disclosure and there must be a “sufficiently specific, cogent and fact-based reason” in order “to tip the balance in favour of disclosure”. The Commission argued that, in the present case, there is no such reason that would tip the balance in favour of releasing the records. Rather, it argued, disclosure of the records would undermine confidence in the confidentiality of the merger review process and could significantly impair its ability to obtain the information required to carry out its functions effectively, which it stated would be contrary to the public interest.
In addition, the Commission made submissions in the context of the public interest test provided for in certain other exemptions in the FOI Act upon which it relied, and I consider it appropriate to include these in an examindation of the public interest test in section 35(3). In particular, it noted that transparency regarding the merger review process is ensured through the publication of Merger Determinations on its website, which it said set out its conclusions and reasoning in respect to mergers. The Commission argued that this ensures an appropriate level of accountability without disclosing material that could prejudice its functions.
The applicant’s submissions
Section 35(1)(a)
In his submissions on section 35(1)(a), the applicant first of all argued that the Commission had erred in withholding the records in full, and that partial release should have been possible, given that a number of records appear to have been created by Commission employees. The applicant argued that section 35(2) of the FOI Act (which provides for the disapplication of section 35(1) in certain circumstances, which I examine further below) should apply to such records.
The applicant argued that the statutory function of the Commission is to promote compliance with, and enforce, competition and consumer protection law in Ireland. He stated that this is distinct from a purely commercial impetus and carries with it, by definition, a higher degree of accountability to the public at large. The applicant argued that this Office should take into account the inherent organisational purpose of the Commission when making its determination.
The public interest test – section 35(3)
In relation to section 35(3), the applicant noted that section 11(3) of the FOI Act requires FOI bodies to have a general regard to the need to achieve greater openness in their activities and to strengthen their accountability and improve the quality of their decision-making. He stated that his purpose in making his FOI request was to understand the reason that an FOI body came to a particular decision, and argued that it followed that the public interest would be better served by the release, rather than the withholding, of the records.
My analysis
Section 35(2)
In circumstances where the applicant argued that section 35(2) is potentially applicable to some of the records, and where (if it applies) section 35(2) would preclude the Commission’s reliance on 35(1) in respect of those records, I take the view that it is appropriate to examine the former provision of the FOI Act first of all. Section 35(2) provides that section 35(1) as a whole shall not apply to a record which was:
(i) prepared by a head, director or member of staff of an FOI body or a service provider;
(ii) prepared in the course of the performance of his or her functions;
(iii) UNLESS disclosure would constitute a breach of a duty of confidence which is owed to a person other than an FOI body, a head, director or member of staff of an FOI body, or a service provider to, an FOI body.
As noted above, the applicant suggested that section 35(2) is potentially engaged in circumstances where certain of the records were prepared by employees of the Commission. I accept that this is the case in respect of the relevant records, and would also note that it seems to be straightforwardly the case the records were prepared by such staff members in the performance of their functions. Thus, I accept that the first two conditions in section 35(2) are met in respect of the relevant records. I make this finding in respect of records 1, 2, and 72 to 92 (in other words all records that were created by staff of the Commission).
The remaining question that I must consider is whether the release of these records would constitute a breach of a duty of confidence that is provided for by an agreement or statute or otherwise by law and is owed by the Commission to a person other than an FOI body or its staff. It is well settled that a duty of confidence provided otherwise by law includes an equitable duty of confidence.
In the Supreme Court decision in the case of Mahon v Post Publications Ltd [2007] 3 I.R. 338 (“the Mahon case”) Fennelly J confirmed that the requirements for a successful action based on a breach of an equitable duty of confidence, at least in a commercial setting, are found in the judgment of Megarry J in Coco v. A. N. Clark (Engineers) Ltd. [1969] R.P.C. 41, at 47:
“[T]hree elements are normally required if, apart from contract, a case of breach ofconfidence is to succeed. First, the information itself ... must 'have the necessaryquality of confidence about it'. Secondly, that information must have been imparted in circumstances importing an obligation of confidence.Thirdly, there must be anunauthorised use of that information to the detriment of the party communicating it."
Fennelly J summarised or restated the requirements of what he called “the contours”
of the equitable doctrine of confidence as follows:
“1. the information must in fact be confidential or secret: it must ... “have the necessary quality of confidence about it”;
2. it must have been communicated by the possessor of the information in circumstances which impose an obligation of confidence or trust on the person receiving it;
3. it must be wrongfully communicated by the person receiving it or by another person who is aware of the obligation of confidence.”
In previous decisions, this Office has stated its understanding that "detriment" could arise simply where the relevant information is disclosed without the consent of the party to whom the information relates.
In the section of its submissions addressing section 35(1)(b) (which relates to the question of the existence of a duty of confidence, and which contains essentially the same test as that set out in section 35(2)), the Commission argued that such a duty exists in this case, and that to release the records would constitute a breach of this duty. It argued that this is the case in circumstances where, in the context of merger reviews, obligations of confidentiality arise both explicitly (through processes and communications) and implicitly, given the sensitive nature of the information provided. It noted that, for the purposes of section 35, the circumstances in which information is provided is of critical importance, and stated that this is particularly relevant in the context of merger reviews. The Commission argued that parties participating in the merger review process must be assured that the information they provide, which is often commercially sensitive in nature, will be treated with the utmost confidentiality. The Commission stated that any perception that such information could be disclosed, including via FOI requests, would fundamentally undermine that assurance and, in turn the willingness of the relevant parties to engage fully with it.
I have examined the records outlined above which were created by staff of the Commission in the performance of their functions. In my view, the records comprising RFIs (in other words records 1, 2, 91 and 92) contain significant amounts of detail regarding the commercial operations of the parties to the merger. In particular, I note that the RFIs refer back to previous information provided to the Commission by the parties, and that this information goes into quite granular detail regarding certain previous agreements signed by the parties. Furthermore, I take the view that record 72 (the Commission’s Phase 2 report on the merger) contains significant and substantial details in relation to the commercial operations of both parties to the merger. Moreover, I consider that the records comprising interviews carried out by the Commission with relevant third parties (records 73 to 90) contain information provided by the third parties relating to their operations and commercial activities. I take the view that the parties to whom this information relates, and who in large part provided the information to the Commission, are entitled to regard the information as having provided in confidence, and that they have a reasonable expectation that the Commission would treat it as confidential. I make this finding where the material in the records that relates to the third parties is, to my mind, information about the commercial workings of the parties, and is in all likelihood commercially sensitive information. I am satisfied that the three-pronged test for the existence of an equitable duty of confidence, as set out by Fennelly J in the Mahon case, is satisfied in respect of this information.
Accordingly, my view is that an equitable duty of confidence exists in respect of the information in these records, and that this duty is owed by the Commission to the relevant third-party commercial entities. In other words, the duty of confidence is owed to parties other than an FOI body, a head, director or member of staff of an FOI body, or a service provider to, an FOI body. Thus, the third requirement for the operation of section 35(2) is not met. I therefore find that section 35(2) of the FOI Act does not operate in this case to preclude the Commission’s reliance on section 35(1).
Section 35(1)(a)
It remains for me to examine whether the records are, in fact, exempt from release under section 35(1)(a).
In relation to the first two requirements of section 35(1)(a), I accept that the information in the records was given to the Commission in confidence and on the understanding that it would be treated as confidential. I am satisfied that this is the case in respect of both the information in the records created by the Commission that pertains to relevant third-party commercial entities, and the information in the remainder of the records that was provided by those entities to the Commission. I make this finding in circumstances where I accept the arguments of the Commission to the effect that both the parties to the merger, and the relevant third parties, have provided (in the context of the merger review process) information which is sensitive regarding their operations, finances and strategies, and their assessments of markets and competitors. I also accept that this information which is not in the public domain. My view is that the Commission’s arguments regarding the first two requirements of section 35(1)(a) effectively state its position that the merger review process is known to the parties involved, and that the information necessary for the Commission to carry out the review can reasonably be regarded by the parties providing it as being confidential information. Essentially, it seems to me that the review process is bought into by the parties engaging with the Commission on the understanding of the confidentiality of the information provided.
I am also satisfied that the third requirement of section 35(1)(a) is met in this case. I am quite prepared to accept that the release of the information in the records that pertains to the commercial operations and inner workings of both the parties to the merger and the third-party entities would be likely to prejudice the giving to it of further similar information. It should be noted in this regard that I am not required to satisfy myself that the disclosure of the information in the records would definitely prejudice the supply of the relevant information, and it is sufficient that disclosure would be likely to prejudice such supply. I am satisfied that this standard is met in this case. In particular, I accept the arguments of the Commission that the release of the records at issue might reasonably be expected to undermine the willingness of future parties to provide it with full and candid information, and that such an outcome might have a direct and detrimental impact on its ability to carry out effective merger reviews. It should be noted that “prejudice” in this context need not mean that, for example, the provision of similar information in future might not occur at all or that the information-gathering process carried out by the Commission in the course of carrying out merger reviews is defeated entirely; it is sufficient that, for example, the quality or timeliness of the information provided might be expected to be adversely impacted. Based on the contents of the records and the arguments of the Commission, I accept that such an expectation is reasonable.
Finally in relation to section 35(1)(a), I accept that the fourth requirement is also met. It seems to me to be self-evident that the type of information at issue is of central importance to the Commission in terms of its ability to effectively carry out merger reviews. Indeed, it is difficult to see how the Commission could perform this function to any meaningful degree should the information it requires for the purpose not be forthcoming for any reason.
Accordingly, on the basis of the analysis above, my view is that each of the four requirements in section 35(1)(a) are met in this case. In particular, I accept the Commission’s arguments that the circumstances in which the information in the records was imparted to it (by the parties to the merger as well as relevant third-party entities) entail a clear mutual expectation of confidentiality. I therefore find that the records at issue are within the scope of the exemption provided for in section 35(1)(a) of the FOI Act.
Section 35(3)
It remains for me to examine whether the public interest would on balance be better served by the granting rather than the withholding of the information in the records, under section 35(3) of the FOI Act.
On the one hand, section 35 itself recognises a public interest in protecting confidentiality. In this case, I accept that there is a public interest in protecting the confidentiality of these particular records, which serves the flow of information from the parties involved in the merger, and other relevant third-party commercial entities, to the Commission. On the other hand, I must consider whether there is a public interest in disclosing the specific content of these records.
In carrying out any review, this Office has regard to the general principles of openness and transparency set out in section 11(3) of the FOI Act, which were highlighted by the applicant in his submissions. As the applicant noted, section 11(3) provides that an FOI body must have regard to the need to achieve greater openness in the activities of FOI bodies and to promote adherence by them to the principles of transparency in government and public affairs and the need to strengthen the accountability and improve the quality of decision making of FOI bodies. However, it is equally the case that, as flagged by the Commission in its submissions, the Supreme Court in the eNet case has found that a general principle of openness does not suffice to direct release of records in the public interest and that “there must be a sufficiently specific, cogent and fact-based reason to tip the balance in favour of disclosure”.
In the applicant’s submissions, he stated that the reason for his FOI request was to try and understand the reasons why the Commission had taken its decision on the merger. I accept that this a valid argument for the purposes of section 35(3). There certainly exists, to my mind, a very valid public interest in knowing how the Commission reaches decisions on merger reviews.
This being said, it should also be noted that the purpose of the FOI Act is not to open up to scrutiny the commercial workings of private entities. While I am quite prepared to accept that a public interest certainly exists in casting greater light on the operations and decision-making processes of the Commission, I do not take the view that this public interest requires the opening up to scrutiny of the commercial and financial details of the parties to the merger and of the relevant third-party commercial entities. Moreover, my view is that the public interest in knowing the reasons for the Commission’s decision is linked to an equally valid public interest in the protection of the consumer (against, for example, the development of monopolies in certain sectors). However, again my view is that this public interest does not entitle the world at large to access information that goes to the inner workings of private companies.
It is relevant, in the context of the public interest I have identified in understanding the reasons for the Commission’s decisions, that – as noted above – the Commission publishes Merger Determinations on its website. These determinations are, to my mind, comprehensive and thorough (for example, the relevant determination report on the Commission website regarding the merger at issue in this case runs to some 260 pages and contain a significant level of detail in relation to the Commission’s investigation, reasoning and findings). My view is that, in publishing detailed Merger Determinations on its website, the Commission is clearly attempting to ensure an appropriate level of transparency regarding its own operations, while at the same time protecting commercially sensitive information relating to private enterprises. I consider that the public interest identified by the applicant is to a large degree met by the Commission’s publication of Merger Determinations.
Accordingly, my finding is that, for the purposes of section 35(3) of the FOI Act, the balance of the public interest favours the withholding, rather than the release, of the records at issue.
My findings
Based on my analysis above, I find that the Commission was justified under section 35(1)(a) of the FOI Act in withholding access in full to the records at issue. In those circumstances, I am not required to examine the extent to which the records might also be exempt from release under the other provisions of the FOI Act upon which the Commission relied.
Decision
Having carried out a review under section 22(2) of the FOI Act, I hereby affirm the decision of the Commission. I find that it was justified under section 35(1)(a) of the FOI Act in refusing access to the records sought.
Right of Appeal
Section 24 of the FOI Act sets out detailed provisions for an appeal to the High Court by a party to a review, or any other person affected by the decision. In summary, such an appeal, normally on a point of law, must be initiated not later than four weeks after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.

title: Ms. X & The The Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage
text:
Decision
Ms. X & The The Department of Housing, Local Government and Heritage
From
Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC)
Case number: OIC-161108-Q2C5X0
Published on 9 July 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Preliminary Matters
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Right of Appeal
Whether the Department was justified in refusing access, under section29(1) of the FOI Act to records of submissions to an interdepartmental consultation process
09 July 2026
Background
The background to this review is the preparation of revised regulations, as part of the phased commencement of the Planning and Development Act 2024 (hereinafter 2024 Act). In February 2025, the Department invited government departments and bodies to make submissions to inform the drafting of updated regulations in relation to Exempted Development and the traffic light approach to Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) screening thresholds. It noted that there would be further opportunity for departments, State bodies and the wider public to make submissions through public consultation. In March 2025, the Department published the related Planning and Development Act 2024 Implementation Plan.
Referencing a specified media article that reported on plans to exempt certain works from planning permission, the applicant submitted a request to the Department for copies of the “ submissions made by the 11 government departments, planning bodies, and local authorities
”.
By decision of 27 June 2025, the Department refused access to all 43 records it identified as coming within the scope of the request under section 29(1) of the FOI Act. It said all of the records are relevant to the deliberative processes underway in relation to the review of exempted development provisions and that pending the conclusion of those deliberative processes, it would be contrary to the public interest to release these records.
On 4 July 2025, the applicant sought an internal review of that decision. On 25 July 2025, the Department affirmed its refusal of the request. On 1 August 2025, the applicant applied to this Office for a review of the Department’s decision. She argued that the Department failed to demonstrate how release of records refused would be contrary to the public interest.
I have now completed my review in accordance with section 22(2) of the FOI Act. In carrying out my review, I have had regard to the correspondence outlined above and to the submissions made by the parties. I have also had regard to the contents of the records at issue. I have decided to conclude this review by way of a formal, binding decision.
Scope of Review
The Department interpreted the applicant’s request broadly, to cover records of submissions made in response to the invitation to make submissions. Records identified related both to EIA screening thresholds and Exempted Development Regulations. In its correspondence with this Office, the Department said Exempted Development Regulations are set out at Schedule 2 of the Planning and Development Regulations 2001 (as amended). It said the Schedule contains approximately 120 classes of development and is not limited to domestic developments. The Department emphasised that housing policy (including domestic planning exemptions) is under its own remit, and departments were invited to review any classes of exemption applicable to their distinct statutory responsibilities i.e. that they, or bodies under their aegis, considered required amendment. I also note that domestic exempted developments was the main feature of the article linked by the applicant in her FOI request. However, the intended purpose of the Department did not preclude submissions on matters outside the direct remit of the respondent departments and bodies, including housing.
Accordingly, this review is concerned solely with the question of whether the Department was justified in refusing access, under section 29(1) of the FOI Act, to the 43 records it identified as coming within the scope of the request.
Preliminary Matters
Section 18(1) provides, that "if it is practicable to do so", access to an otherwise exempt record shall be granted by preparing a copy, in such form as the head of the public body concerned considers appropriate, of the record with the exempt information removed. Section 18(1) does not apply, however, if the copy provided for thereby would be misleading (section 18(2) refers). It should be noted that the Commissioner takes the view that, generally, neither the definition of a record nor the provisions of section 18 envisage or require the extracting of particular sentences or occasional paragraphs from the remainder of a record for the purpose of granting access to those particular sentences or paragraphs.
Analysis and Findings
Section 29(1)
Section 29(1) provides for the refusal of a request if (a) the record concerned contains matter relating to the deliberative process of an FOI body, including opinions, advice, recommendations and the results of consultations considered by the body for the purpose of those processes, and (b) the body considers that the granting of the request would be contrary to the public interest. These are two independent requirements and the fact that the first is met carries no presumption that the second is met.
Section 29(1)(a)
For section 29(1)(a) to apply, the records must contain matter relating to the ‘deliberative process’ of an FOI body. An FOI body relying on this exemption should identify both the deliberative process concerned and any matter in particular which relates to that process. A deliberative process may be described as a thinking process which informs decision making in FOI bodies. It involves the gathering of information from a variety of sources and weighing or considering carefully all of the information and facts obtained with a view to making a decision or reflecting upon the reasons for or against a particular choice. Thus, it involves the consideration of various matters with a view to making a decision on a particular matter. It would, for example, include some weighing up or evaluation of competing options or the consideration of proposals or courses of action. The fact that a deliberative process exists and is ongoing does not mean that the exemption automatically applies without consideration of all the provisions of section 29. Equally, the fact that a deliberative process is at an end does not mean that the exemption can no longer apply.
In its submissions to this Office the Department said the records were submitted by Government Departments and bodies under their aegis in advance of the general public consultation on exempted development and were in response to the circulation of an issues paper by the Department on 24 February 2025 to all Government Departments. It said the records are related to the Department’s respective policy areas and functions of bodies under their Aegis. It said engagement is still ongoing with these bodies as is the requirement of section 4(3) of the Act of 2024 as any changes to legislation may impact the function of Departments and their bodies.
Section 4(3) of the 2024 Act provides that the Minister shall, before making regulations under the Act, consult with any State authority in which functions vest that he or she considers are connected with the matters to which the proposed regulations relate. The issues paper referenced explains that the 2024 Act was signed into law on 17 October 2024 and that an Implementation Plan which would set out the arrangements to implement a phased commencement of the 2024 Act to facilitate the transition to the new legislation across the planning system had been finalised and would be published shortly. It explains that a key part of the arrangements to commence the 2024 Act is preparation of revised regulations to replace the regulations that underpin the Planning and Development Act 2000, as amended (the 2000 Act). It notes that the existing provisions in the 2000 Act will remain in place until the relevant provisions in the 2024 Act are commenced. It explains that the Department is in the process of preparing these updated regulations and that two key sets of regulations will deal with exempted development and also the proposed introduction of a traffic light approach to setting Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) thresholds. It explains that the aim of the paper is to provide Government Departments (in consultation with State Bodies under their aegis) as well as the local government sector an opportunity to advise the Department of any policies or requirements which may be relevant to the preparation of regulations on exempted development and the proposed introduction of a traffic light approach to setting EIA screening thresholds.
Having considered the Department’s submissions and having examined the records, I accept that the records relate to a deliberative process. I find, therefore, that the requirements of section 29(1)(a) are met. However, that is not the end of the matter as I must also consider whether granting access to the record would be contrary to the public interest, pursuant to section 29(1)(b).
Section 29(1)(b)
The public interest test at section 29(1)(b) is a strong test, requiring the FOI body to show that the granting of the request would be contrary to the public interest, and is stronger than the public interest test in many other sections of the Act, which generally requires that the public interest would, on balance, be better served by granting than by refusing to grant the request. This Office accepts that the FOI Act clearly envisages that there will be cases in which disclosure of the details of an FOI body’s deliberations – whether before or, in some cases, after a decision based on those deliberations has been made – would be against the public interest. However, that is not to say that such disclosure is always, as a matter of principle, against the public interest. Any arguments against release under section 29 should be substantiated and supported by the facts of the case. An FOI body should show how granting access to the particular record would be contrary to the public interest, e.g. by identifying a specific harm to the public interest flowing from release.
Timing of release is relevant to consideration of section 29(1)(b). However, the fact that a deliberative process exists and is ongoing does not mean that the exemption automatically applies. Equally, the fact that a deliberative process is at an end does not mean that the exemption automatically does not apply.
The applicant submitted that an ongoing deliberative process did not equate to an automatic exemption from release and that the Department failed to demonstrate that it would be contrary to the public interest to release the record. She argued that informed public debate about a subject of significant public interest, involving considerations around housing standards and affordability, climate considerations around compact development, is significantly in the public interest. She noted that government ministers have been debating in public the issues under consideration, and she argued that if that doesn't impede the decision-making process, it is hard to see how releasing these documents would.
During the review, this Office’s Investigator sought to clarify the status of the deliberations. The Department submitted that the deliberative process was ongoing in respect of all relevant records. Though its precise submissions varied in relation to the strands of regulatory reform at issue, it was consistent in its position that the deliberative process was ongoing. It said the submissions by Departments and State Bodies relate to policies and functions under the remit of those bodies. It said the possible amendment of planning legislation which could impact and alter the functions of State Bodies requires detailed consideration. It said the process for public scrutiny of Exempted Development legislation is through the Oireachtas which is only finalised once any proposed legislation is approved by both Houses of the Oireachtas. It said the deliberative process is therefore ongoing until the legislation reaches the Oireachtas and said it is inappropriate to provide inaccurate information as engagement is ongoing.
As regards Exempted Development regulations, at the time of its submission the Department said all such regulations were “ at various stages of the drafting process and require screening to determine if a full Strategic Environmental Assessment or Appropriate Assessment is required
.” It said that following environmental assessment, the regulations will “… proceed for formal ratification by resolution of both Houses of the Oireachtas, following referral to the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Housing
.”
Responding to the Investigator’s query regarding a government Press Release of 21 April 2026, titled Government announces changes to Planning Exemptions Regulations which appeared to indicate a concluded deliberative process, it said proposed amendments to domestic/residential exemptions was only one element of the overall exempted development regulations, and residential exemptions were being progressed under the 2000 Act in advance of the commencement of equivalent provisions under the 2024 Act.
During the review, Regulations regarding domestic planning exemptions progressed, and the Department has now clarified that several domestic draft regulations were prioritised and have been referred to the Joint Oireachtas Committee on Housing, Local Government and Heritage for consideration on 14 July 2026. It said it regards the deliberative process as ongoing with respect to these regulations and highlighted that these regulations, relating to housing, are under the Department’s own remit.
As regards EIA regulations, the Department said, at the time of its submission, that a review of the EIA screening thresholds was ongoing, and preparations were being made to progress a public consultation. The Department said it expected the public consultation would be open for submissions in Q2 2026.
The applicant’s submissions regarding the public interest test at section 29 were put to the Department. As to how release of the records at issue would be contrary to the public interest, the Department said it needs appropriate time and space to deliberate and decide on this matter, and it argued that the public interest would not be served by any action that might hinder the Department’s deliberative processes. It said that until a policy or action is agreed between relevant stakeholders, the discussion remains internal. It argued that granting the request would be contrary to the public interest as it may negatively impact on the operation of Departments and State Bodies in the carrying out of their function by providing a false narrative of what may or may not be in final legislation. It said that providing information which is not yet finalised / decided upon may have unintended consequences such as creating an anomaly for certain types of development by either artificially increasing or decreasing the number of planning applications. It said the planning system deals with over 30,000 planning applications annually. It said that only once legislation is approved by the Minister and in the case of Exempted Development, approved by positive resolution of the Houses of the Oireachtas, can it become law. It argued, therefore, that prematurely publishing information contained within the deliberative process may create a false narrative as the deliberative process is not yet finalised.
The Department’s response was requested on the applicant’s submission that the matter was addressed by politicians and covered in the media. The Department made a distinction between the records at issue which concerned other departments and bodies, and its own policies. It said that while some information in relation to certain proposed exemptions has been discussed in the media, this was in relation to policy issues which come under the remit of the Department and do not relate to policies of other government departments or agencies.
Responding to the applicant’s submission that release of the records was in the public interest and would lead to “informed public debate about a subject of significant public interest”, the Department highlighted that public consultation provided an opportunity for private individuals and organisations to make submissions on exempted development, including relating to residential development. The Department clarified that the public consultation (regarding Exempted Development Regulations) yielded approximately 900 submissions, and it is understood that copies will be published to the Government website by 30 September 2026. It restated the distinction between its own policy and submissions.
Analysis
In the course of this analysis, I have had regard to public-facing information. I note that in terms of publication arrangements, there appears to be a material distinction between publication of submissions to public consultation processes as opposed to submissions to an interdepartmental consultation process. The Public Consultation Principles & Guidance of the Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation place an emphasis on publication of public consultation responses in order to create a “legislative footprint”. However, I am not aware of any equivalent guidance for publication of submissions to an interdepartmental consultation. The Issues Paper furnished to this Office instructed that government Departments could make additional submissions to a public consultation process, and I note the guidance to both public consultations included that submissions may be published. The Issues Paper and request for submissions to this consultation process did not contain the same points of information as the public consultations as regards potential publication.
I have fully considered the parties’ submissions and the records at issue. I note that Regulations regarding EIA and Exempted Developments are at different stages.
Noting the Department’s submission on the status of EIA Regulations, I consider that the process of regulatory reform is at a relatively early stage. I note that at the time of writing, the public consultation process has only recently closed. Regarding Exempted Development Regulations, my understanding of the Department’s submission is that the regulations are at a more advanced stage relative to EIA regulations. The Department initially submitted that all Exempted Development Regulations are at “ various stages of the drafting process
” and that following drafting and environmental screening/ assessment, the regulations will go before the Oireachtas. As set out above, at the time of writing, some draft regulations will shortly go before an Oireachtas Committee.
The applicant has submitted that the public interest would be served by the release of the records. Section 29(1)(b) does not require me to consider whether the weight of the public interest favouring disclosure of the records is greater than the weight of the public interest favouring the withholding of the records. Rather, it requires that disclosure “would be contrary to the public interest”.
Having considered the parties’ submissions, I accept that the process of policy formation and regulatory reform is complex, that the Department needs appropriate time and space to deliberate and decide on matters, and that any action that might hinder the Department’s deliberative processes is contrary to the public interest.
Insofar as the records relate to EIA Regulations, I accept the Department’s submission that release of records relating to EIA Regulations would be contrary to the public interest. This deliberative process is not only ongoing, but also at a relatively early stage, and I agree that the Department requires space to engage with Departments and bodies.
Insofar as the records relate to Exempted Development Regulations, I consider that drafting and pre-legislative scrutiny are fluid, deliberative processes. While elements of a legislative approach would have been deliberated on in order the inform such processes, I accept the deliberative process is still ongoing. As release of records under FOI is equivalent to their publication to the world at large, I accept that release may hinder this deliberative process. I consider the Department’s submission regarding potential misinformation in the context of planning exemptions, specifically, the potential harm of artificially increasing or decreasing the number of planning applications, to be sufficiently cogent and fact-based to meet the requirements of section 29 (1)(b).
I note that the Department previously stated the deliberative process was ongoing until the legislation reaches the Oireachtas which appears to contradict its subsequent position that the deliberative process is ongoing with respect to regulations shortly before an Oireachtas Committee. However, the Department has clarified that the Oireachtas Committee is a form of pre-legislative scrutiny. I accept this distinction.
In light of the above, I accept that disclosure of the records would be contrary to the public interest. I find that the second requirement of section 29(1), as set out at section 29(1)(b) of the FOI Act, has been met.
Section 29(2) – exceptions
Section 29(2) provides that subsection (1) does not apply to a record if and in so far as it contains any or all of the following:
a) matter such as rules, procedures, guidelines, interpretations and precedents used, or intended to be used, by an FOI body for the purpose of making decisions, determinations or recommendations;
b) factual information;
c) the reasons for the making of a decision by an FOI body;
d) a report of an investigation or analysis of the performance, efficiency or effectiveness of an FOI body in relation to the functions generally or a particular function of the body;
e) a report, study or analysis of a scientific or technical expert relating to the subject of his or her expertise or a report containing opinions or advice of such an expert and not being a report used or commissioned for the purposes of a decision of an FOI body made pursuant to any enactment or scheme.
The applicant submitted that the identified records “likely include "factual information" and analysis, which would make them non-exempt.” The Department was requested to clarify its position as to whether the records contained non-exempt information as specified at section 29(2) of the FOI Act. In response the Department said the submissions consist of issues for discussion, draft material and observations." Having examined the records, I consider they do contain severable factual information as follows:
Record No.
Description of factual information
Record 5
Page 1, paras. 2-3
Record 8
Text under Heading A1, A2 (except final two sentences), A4, text under heading 1, except last sentence, text under heading two, except last sentence.
Record 11
Page 1, paras. 3-4, Page 2, para. 1
Record 15
Page 2, paras. 2 - 3; Page 4, para. 2 (i.e. para. 1 under heading 2.0)
Record 21
Page 1, paras. 2 - 4, 6
Record 22
Pages 1-2, all information at heading 2.0
Record 29
Page 2, Para 1, excluding fist sentence
Record 34
Page 2, all text under sub-heading “introduction”, Page 3, paras. 1-3.
I find section 29(2)(b) applies to the above-specified information. I direct release of same.
Having regard to the remainder of the records, while I accept that the records contain factual information, it is relevant that the factual information is, in other instances inextricably linked to other types of information such as analysis, opinions, etc. I have already outlined the provisions of section 18 of the FOI Act and the Commissioner’s approach to the matter. In my view, it would not be practicable to attempt to further extract any factual information from these records while at the same time ensuring that the redacted copies are not misleading under section 18 of the Act. With respect to these records, I find that section 29(2)(b) does not apply.
Further to the above, I am satisfied that none of the other provisions of section 29(2) apply in this case.
Decision
Having carried out a review under section 22(2) of the FOI Act I hereby vary the decision of the Department. I find that section 29(2)(b) applies to certain specified records as specified in this decision and, I direct release of same. I find that the Department was justified in refusing to release the remainder of records of submissions to a consultation process under section 29(1) of the Act.
Right of Appeal
Section 24 of the FOI Act sets out detailed provisions for an appeal to the High Court by a party to a review, or any other person affected by the decision. In summary, such an appeal, normally on a point of law, must be initiated by the requester not later than eight weeks after notice of the decision was given, and by any other party not later than four weeks after notice of the decision was given.
Stephen Rafferty
Senior Investigator

title: Mr. X & The Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation
text:
Decision
Mr. X & The Department of Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation
From
Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC)
Case number: OIC-200088-A0A0G2
Published on 9 July 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Preliminary Matters
My Analysis
Decision
Right of Appeal
Whether the Department was justified in refusing the applicant’s request for further records relating to a decision not to approve increases to the pensions of medical scientists who retired prior to 1 January 2024 under section 15(1)(a) of the FOI Act, on the grounds that no relevant records were found after all reasonable steps were carried out to locate them
9 July 2026
Background
In a request dated 1 September 2025 (with the agreed wording and timeline finalised on 9 September 2025), the applicant sought access to all records in relation to the Department’s decision not to approve the application of pay increases to the pensions of medical scientists who retired prior to 1 January 2024 as per the recommendation contained in the Conal Devine Medical Scientist Grades Assessment report published in January 2023. The Department interpreted the timeline of this request to be for records dating from 1 January 2023 to 3 April 2024.
It is noted that the applicant submitted a substantially similar request to the Department of Health for which a decision is also issuing by today’s date (Case number OIC-200087-A0A0G1, available on our website at
www.oic.ie
).
On 29 September 2025, the Department made a decision to grant the applicant’s request. The Department identified one record, a short email thread between the Department, the HSE, and the Department of Health from March 2024, as falling within the scope of the applicant’s request and released this in full.
On 10 October 2025, the applicant sought an internal review of the Department’s decision. The applicant said that that the email thread released by the Department did not provide him with the relevant information he was looking for. The applicant said he was seeking records showing who made and signed off on the decision not to award the increase granted under the Devine Report to medical scientists who retired prior to the 1 January 2024. The applicant said that, given that the Minister has statutory responsibility for approving pay increases to pensioners, it is inconceivable that no departmental records exist around this matter.
On 22 October 2025, the Department’s internal reviewer affirmed its original decision.
On 19 January 2026, the applicant applied to this Office for a review of the Department’s decision. In submissions to this Office dated 9 February 2026, the applicant said that the denial of the relevant increase recommended in the Conal Devine report is in breach of the Department’s guidelines on pay parity (referenced P18-13-2018) dated 24 September 2024. He said that it is also in breach of a guarantee given by the Department’s Deputy Secretary General to ICTU on 1 February 2024 that if a wage agreement was accepted the current policy of maintaining parity between pay of serving staff and pensions awarded under pre-existing public service pension schemes would be extended for the duration of the new pay agreement 2024-2026.
I have now completed my review in accordance with section 22(2) of the FOI Act. In carrying out my review, I have had regard to the submissions made by the Department and the applicant. I have decided to conclude this review by way of a formal, binding decision.
Scope of Review
The Department’s position is that no further relevant records exist or can be found within the scope of the applicant’s request. This is, in essence, a refusal to grant access to further relevant records under section 15(1)(a) of the FOI Act, which provides for the refusal of a request where the records sought do not exist or cannot be found.
Accordingly, this review is concerned solely with whether the Department was justified in refusing access, under section 15(1)(a), to further records falling within the scope of the applicant’s request.
Preliminary Matters
Before addressing the substantive matters relating to this review, I would like to address some preliminary matters.
First, it is important to note that a review by this Office is considered to be “ de novo
”, which means that in this case, it is based on the circumstances and the law as they pertain at the time of my decision and is not confined to the basis upon which the FOI body reached its decision.
Secondly, it is important to note that section 13(4) of the FOI Act provides that in deciding whether to grant or refuse a request, any reason that the requester gives for the request shall be disregarded. This means that I cannot have regard to the applicant’s motives for seeking access to the information in question, except in so far as those motives reflect what might be regarded as genuine public interest factors in favour of release of the information where the FOI Act requires a consideration of the public interest (not relevant in this case).
Thirdly, the FOI Act provides for the access to records that are actually held. It does not provide for a right of access to records which ought to exist. With one exception, which does not apply here, the FOI Act does not require FOI bodies to create a record if none exists.
Finally, it is also important to note that this Office has no remit to investigate complaints, to adjudicate on how FOI bodies perform their functions generally, or to act as an alternative dispute resolution mechanism with respect to actions taken by FOI bodies.
Analysis and Findings
Section 15(1)(a)
Section 15(1)(a) of the Act provides for the refusal of a request where the records sought do not exist or cannot be found after all reasonable steps to ascertain their whereabouts have been taken. The role of this Office in a case such as this is to review the decision of the FOI body and to decide whether that decision was justified. This means that I must have regard to the evidence available to the decision maker and to the reasoning used by the decision maker in arriving at his/her decision and also must assess the adequacy of the searches conducted by the FOI body in looking for relevant records.
Department’s submissions
In its submissions to this Office, by way of background, the Department said that
in 2023, the Labour Court recommended the implementation of the findings of the Report on Medical Scientist Grades Assessment (also known as the Devine report) no later than 1 January 2024. It said that this recommendation then formed part of the negotiations which culminated in the Public Service Pay Agreement 2024-2026. The Department further said that Circular 2/2024 set forth new rates for the Medical Scientist grades that were applied to existing staff with effect from 1 January 2024. It said this constituted a regrading and a move to a new scale for the relevant staff. It said that it is established practice that in such cases, any attendant pay increases are not passed on to those who retired before its implementation.
The Department said that it understood the applicant’s request to relate to records concerning the application of pay increases to the pensions of medical scientists who retired prior to 1 January 2024 as a result of the 2023 Labour Court recommendation. The Department said that the relevant business areas for this request were Pay and Industrial Relations and the Public Service Pensions Policy Unit. It said that the request was primarily dealt with by staff responsible for health pay and industrial relations in the Pay & Industrial Relations Unit in Public Sector Resourcing Division.
The Department said that staff in its Public Service Pensions Policy Unit of Work and Pensions Division were asked to search for any relevant records. It said that searches were conducted of staff email inboxes and folders, network shared drives, and eDocs file management system to identify relevant records. The key terms the Department said it used in the searches included: “ pensions
”, “ medical scientists
”, “ Conal
”, “ Devine
”, “ MLSA
”, “pensioners” and “award” between 1 January 2023 to 3 April 2024.
The Department further said that, where relevant, manual searches were conducted to identify if any hard copy files existed. It said that a Microsoft Excel file listing hard copy files was examined and no records relevant to the applicant’s request were identified. The Department also said it also manually searched files in the office and no hard copy records were identified.
As a result of all searches, the Department said that the only relevant record identified was the email thread it released to the applicant. It said no further records were identified to be within the remit of the request.
The Department also specifically addressed a number of queries put by the Investigating Officer assigned to this case. More particularly, the Investigating Officer had asked the Department if it holds any records showing who made and signed off on the decision not to award the increase granted under the Devine Report to medical scientists who retired prior to the 1 January 2024. In response, the Department said that no records exist of a “ decision not to award the increase granted under the Devine Report to medical scientists who retired prior to the 1 January 2024
” as an established policy exists that provided for the relevant outcome in this matter. The Department said established public service pension policy dictates that where a post is upgraded, the terms of the upgrade apply from the date of the sanctioned upgrade. The Department said that this does not apply retrospectively to previous postholders, either employees who formerly held the post or retirees who previously held the post. It said this pertains across all grades of staff across the public service. The Department provided a link to its website which outlines this policy -
https://assets.gov.ie/static/documents/application-of-pay-parity-as-pension-increase-policy-in-line-with-the-public-service-a.pdf
The Investigating Officer also sought further information from the Department as to whether any meetings or discussions which took place in relation to a decision not to approve the application of pay increases to the pensions of medical scientists who retired prior to 1 January 2024 and, if so, were there any record of such meetings or discussions. In response, the Department said no record of any meetings or discussions was found during the search for records.
Finally, the Department said that it considered that the pensions referred to in the applicant’s request are likely governed by the HSE Employee Superannuation Scheme. It said that pension increases under this scheme are governed by Section 13 which states " The Executive may grant such increases in such pensions and preserved pensions under this Scheme as may be authorised from time to time by the Minister with the consent of the Minister for Finance
" (now the Minister for Health and the Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation). The Department said that any adjustment to the terms and conditions, which would include pensions, of any grade of staff would require the approval of itself and the Department of Health.
Applicant’s submissions
The Investigating Officer provided the applicant with a summary of the Department’s submissions as outlined above and invited the applicant to make further submissions of his own which he duly did.
In response, the applicant said that the Department’s submissions referred to regrading/upgrading which he said is the first mention of this and was not part of the terms of reference of the Devine Report. The applicant said there has been no prior mention of regrading/upgrading in any of the documents released by the Department. The applicant said that as different rules regarding pensions apply to special pay awards and upgrade/regrade, the classification of the increases under the Devine Report is fundamental to his FOI request. He said that it is inconceivable that a decision of this importance has not been documented and apparently no records of it exist in the Department.
My Analysis
It is important to note that the FOI Act does not require absolute certainty as to the existence or location of records, as situations can arise where records are lost or simply cannot be found. What the FOI Act requires is that the public body concerned takes all reasonable steps to locate relevant records. Furthermore, it is open to this Office to find that an FOI body has satisfied the requirements of section 15(1)(a), even where records that an applicant believes ought to exist, or are known to have existed in the past, have not been located. We do not generally expect FOI bodies to carry out extensive or indefinite general searches for records simply because an applicant asserts that records sought ought to exist or did exist.
The question I must consider, therefore, is whether the Department has taken all reasonable steps to ascertain the whereabouts of the specific records sought.
The Department’s position is that having carried out searches, no records, beyond the email thread already released to the applicant, within the scope of the request exist or can be found. The applicant is not satisfied that all relevant records have been identified and released.
Having carefully considered the Department’s submissions in this matter, I am satisfied that it has provided a sufficiently detailed and cogent explanation as to why no further records exist. In particular, I am satisfied that the Department has carried out all reasonable steps to search for records relevant to the applicant’s request. I am further satisfied that the Department’s explanation of an established policy whereby public service post regrades/upgrades do not apply retrospectively to previous postholders, whether it be employees who formerly held the post, or retirees who previously held the post, adequately explains why no formal decision was taken by the Department as referred to in the applicant’s request. While I acknowledge the applicant’s arguments in his application and submissions that relevant records ought to exist, in the absence of any evidence to suggest that further searches are warranted in this case, I am satisfied that the Department has carried out all reasonable steps to search for and provide the relevant records which are within the scope of the applicant’s request.
Accordingly, I find that the Department was justified in refusing access to records within the scope of the request under section 15(1)(a) of the Act on the basis that the records do not exist or cannot be found after all reasonable steps to ascertain their whereabouts have been taken.
Decision
Having carried out a review under section 22(2) of the FOI Act, I hereby affirm the Department’s decision to refuse the release of further records within the scope of applicant’s request under section 15(1)(a), on the grounds that the Department carried out all reasonable steps to locate all relevant records.
Right of Appeal
Section 24 of the FOI Act sets out detailed provisions for an appeal to the High Court by a party to a review, or any other person affected by the decision. In summary, such an appeal, normally on a point of law, must be initiated not later than four weeks after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
____________________
Mary Connery
Investigator
