title: Mr. X & The Department of Health (the Department)
text:
Decision
Mr. X & The Department of Health (the Department)
From
Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC)
Case number: OIC-200087-A0A0G1
Published on 9 July 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Preliminary Matters
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Right of Appeal
Whether the Department was justified in refusing the applicant’s request for records relating to its decision not to approve increases to the pensions of medical scientists who retired prior to 1 January 2024 under section 15(1)(a) of the FOI Act, on the grounds that no relevant records were found after all reasonable steps were carried out to locate them
9 July 2026
Background
In a request dated 28 August 2025, the applicant sought records of all records relating to the Department’s decision not to approve the application of pay increases to the pensions of medical scientists who retired prior to 1 January 2024 as per the recommendations contained in the Conal Devine Medical Scientist Assessment Report published in January 2023.
On 17 September 2025, the Department refused the applicant’s request on the basis of section 15(1)(a) of the FOI Act, on the grounds that the records concerned do not exist or cannot be found after all reasonable steps to ascertain their whereabouts have been taken. The Department said that it had conducted electronic searches and engaged in discussions with internal colleagues to search for records relevant to the applicant’s request and had determined that none existed. It further said that no formal decision was either made by it or recommended to it in respect of increases to the pensions of medical scientist retirees as the matter is governed centrally under Department of Public Expenditure Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation (hereafter referred to as the Department of Public Expenditure) policy.
On 6 October 2025, the applicant requested an internal review of the Department’s decision. The applicant said that he had made a similar FOI request to the Department of Public Expenditure (a decision also issued in this case numbered OIC-200088-A0A0G1 by today’s date and is available on our website at
www.oic.ie
) which provided him records of email correspondence between the Health Service Executive (HSE), the Department of Public Expenditure, and the Department of Health during March 2024 on this issue. The applicant said that, given that the Minister has statutory responsibility for approving pay increases to pensioners, it is inconceivable that no departmental records exist around this matter.
On 3 December 2025, the Department issued its internal review decision to affirm its original decision to refuse the request under section 15(1)(a). The Department reiterated that it did not make a decision regarding the application of pay increases to the pensions of medical scientists who retired prior to 1 January 2024. The Department quoted from the recommendation of the Labour Court LCR23079, saying:
“It is apparent from Department of Health Circular 2/2004 that the Minister for Health did not make a decision increasing the pension entitlements of those medical scientist pensioners who had retired before 1 January 2024 in line with the revised salary scales that came into effect for medical scientists in post on 1 January 2024.”
However, the Department said that in the interests of full transparency, it provided the applicant with a record showing its side of the discussion with the Department of Public Expenditure, and the Department of Public Expenditure’s guidance on this matter. The Department of Health also provided the applicant with a letter sent to the Medical Laboratory Scientists Association outlining the Department of Health, Health Service Executive and Department of Public Expenditure’s combined position on this topic.
On 19 January 2026, the applicant applied to this Office for a review of the Department’s decision. On 9 February 2026, the applicant informed this Office that he had made a third similar request for the records to the HSE Pensions Management. The applicant said that the HSE informed him that it does not hold the requested records, but the records would be held by the Department of Health. The applicant said that it is strange that there were fundamental changes made to his pension and yet there are no records held by the Department or the HSE Pensions Management on this matter.
I have now completed my review in accordance with section 22(2) of the FOI Act. In carrying out my review, I have had regard to the submissions made by the Department and the applicant. I have decided to conclude this review by way of a formal, binding decision.
Scope of Review
The scope of this review is solely concerned with whether the Department was justified in its decision to refuse the applicant’s request for records relating to the Department’s decision not to approve the application of pay increases to the pensions of medical scientists who retired prior to 1 January 2024 under section 15(1)(a), on the grounds that no relevant records exist or were found after all reasonable steps were taken to locate them.
Preliminary Matters
It is important to note that the role of this Office is not to determine what records should exist, to adjudicate on how FOI bodies perform their functions generally, nor to act as an alternative dispute resolution mechanism with respect to actions taken by FOI bodies, or by any other parties. Our role is confined to reviewing the decision taken by the FOI body on the applicant’s request for records.
Analysis and Findings
Section 15(1)(a)
Section 15(1)(a) of the Act provides for the refusal of a request where the records sought do not exist or cannot be found after all reasonable steps to ascertain their whereabouts have been taken. The role of this Office in a case such as this is to review the decision of the FOI body and to decide whether that decision was justified. This means that I must have regard to the evidence available to the decision maker and to the reasoning used by the decision maker in arriving at his/her decision and also must assess the adequacy of the searches conducted by the FOI body in looking for relevant records.
The evidence in “search” cases generally consists of the steps actually taken to search for the records along with miscellaneous and other information about the record management practices of the FOI body, insofar as those practices relate to the records in question. It is important to note that the FOI Act is concerned with access to records that a public body holds as opposed to records that a requester considers ought to exist.
Department’s submissions
In its submissions to this Office, the Department said it understood the applicant’s request to comprise a request for records relating to a potential “decision” with respect to the pensions of retired medical scientists.
It said that following receipt of the applicant’s request, inbox searches were conducted by relevant parties for email and letter correspondence relevant to the applicant’s request. It further said that searches were conducted of its EDocs system in respect of any additional documents. However, the Department said that the only related information contained on EDocs were circulars, which are publicly available. The Department said that there was a small number of Departmental officials who would have been involved in either the relevant negotiations and/or circular drafting and publication. It said that all such staff were consulted and all records were searched.
The Department further said that following its decision dated 17 September 2025, a Departmental official spoke with the applicant to explain why his request was refused. It said that this staff member outlined exactly what type of documents did exist and indicated that, while the Department did not consider that such records fell within the scope of the applicant’s request as they was did not relate to a decision that the Department had made, it was nonetheless willing to furnish such documents to the applicant if he so wished. It said that as part of its processing of the applicant’s request for an internal review these documents, while not directly relevant to the request, were provided to the applicant in the interest of transparency.
In conclusion, the Department said that it does not have the sole authority to make such a decision as referred to in the applicant’s request. It said that this responsibility sits with the Department of Public Expenditure and, as such, there were no records relevant to the specific wording of the applicant’s request held by the Department of Health. However, the Department said it is available to engage again with the applicant to refine search terms or provide additional information if sought.
Applicant’s submissions
The Investigating Officer provided the applicant with a summary of the Department’s position as outlined above and provided the applicant with the opportunity to make further submissions of his own.
In response, the applicant said that he is satisfied that the Department is honest in its submissions.
My Analysis
It is important to note that the FOI Act does not require absolute certainty as to the existence or location of records. What the FOI Act requires is that the public body concerned takes all reasonable steps to locate relevant records.
The question I must consider, therefore, is whether the Department has taken all reasonable steps to ascertain the whereabouts of the specific records sought.
The Department’s position is that it holds no records that it comes within the scope of the applicant’s request.
Having carefully considered the Department’s submissions in this matter, I am satisfied that it has provided a sufficiently detailed and cogent explanation as to why no records exist. I accept the Department’s position that it does not have the sole authority to make such a decision as not approving the application of pay increases to the pensions of medical scientists. I also accept that the Department did not actually make a decision in this regard.
In the absence of any evidence to suggest that further searches are warranted in this case, I am satisfied that the Department has carried out all reasonable steps to search for relevant records which are within the scope of the applicant’s request.
Accordingly, I find that the Department was justified in refusing access to records within the scope of the request under section 15(1)(a) of the Act on the basis that the records do not exist or cannot be found after all reasonable steps to ascertain their whereabouts have been taken.
Decision
Having carried out a review under section 22(2) of the FOI Act, I hereby affirm the Department’s decision to refuse the applicant’s request under section 15(1)(a) of the FOI Act on the basis that the records do not exist or cannot be found after it had taken all reasonable steps to ascertain their whereabouts.
Right of Appeal
Section 24 of the FOI Act sets out detailed provisions for an appeal to the High Court by a party to a review, or any other person affected by the decision. In summary, such an appeal, normally on a point of law, must be initiated not later than four weeks after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
____________________
Mary Connery
Investigator

title: Ms. Y & Children’s Health Ireland (CHI)
text:
Decision
Ms. Y & Children’s Health Ireland (CHI)
From
Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC)
Case number: OIC-200043-A0A0D3
Published on 9 July 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Right of Appeal
Whether CHI was justified in refusing access to further records relating to the applicant’s son under section 15(1)(a) of the FOI Act
9 July 2026
Background
In a request dated 28 October 2025, the applicant sought access to all records relating to her son from December 2024 to the date of her request.
In a decision dated 14 November 2025, CHI part-granted the applicant’s request. It refused access to parts of her son’s healthcare file under section 15(1)(i)(i) as these records had previously been provided to her. However, it released a number of additional records to the applicant which had been created since it previously provided her son’s medical record to her.
On 8 December 2025 the applicant sought an internal review of CHI’s decision. In her request for an internal review, the applicant argued that her son’s medical records were only a portion of the records sought.
In a letter dated 19 December 2025, CHI affirmed its original decision to refuse access to records under section 15(1)(i)(i).
On 5 January 2026, the applicant applied to this Office for a review of CHI’s decision.
Upon receipt of the applicant’s application to this Office, the Investigating Officer sought clarification from the applicant on the scope of her request and her application for a review by this Office. By response on 1 June 2026, the applicant said she is not seeking a review of the records already released to her by CHI under the Data Protection Act 2018 and confirmed that these records were in her possession. She clarified that she would prefer to limit the scope of her application to any further records falling within the scope of her request outside of what may be considered her son’s medical records. She identified a number of records that she believes ought to exist, such as internal and external correspondence from the relevant time period and which relate to her son.
After clarifying the scope of the applicant’s request, the Investigating Officer invited CHI to make submissions justifying its decision on the applicant’s request. CHI said it did not wish to make any submissions on the matter.
I have now completed my review in accordance with section 22(2) of the FOI Act. In carrying out my review, I have had regard to the correspondence as outlined above. I have decided to conclude this review by way of a formal, binding decision.
Scope of Review
I note that the applicant is of the view that further records relating to her request ought to exist in addition to those records which were provided to her following a Subject Access Request (SAR) under GDPR legislation. In essence, although not explicitly relied upon to refuse access to records, this case involves a search issue under section 15(1)(a) of the FOI Act. I further note the applicant does not dispute that she received records relating to her son under a separate access regime to the FOI Act and has excluded those records from the scope of this review.
Accordingly, this review is concerned solely with whether CHI was justified in refusing the applicant’s request for further records relating to her son under section 15(1)(a) on the basis that further records do not exist or cannot be found after it took all reasonable steps to identify and ascertain the whereabouts of same.
Analysis and Findings
Section 15(1)(a)
Section 15(1)(a) provides for the refusal of a request where the records sought do not exist or cannot be found after all reasonable steps to ascertain their whereabouts have been taken. The role of this Office is to review the decision of the FOI body and to decide whether that decision was justified. We have regard to the relevant information available and assess the adequacy of the searches conducted by the FOI body.
The question I must consider, therefore, is whether CHI has taken all reasonable steps to ascertain the whereabouts of the records sought by the applicant.
It is important to note that a review by this Office is considered to be “de novo", which means that in this case, it is based on the circumstances and the law as they pertain at the time of my decision and is not confined to the basis upon which the FOI body reached its decision.
As noted above, CHI did not provide this Office with any submissions in support of its decision, nor did it address any of the queries put to it by the Investigating Officer with respect to the searches it had conducted for records relevant to the applicant’s request. I therefore have no information before me on which to base a finding that it has carried out all reasonable steps to search for and provide the relevant records which are within the scope of the applicant’s request.
Accordingly, having regard to the information before this Office, and in the absence of any submissions from the FOI Body in this case, I simply cannot find that CHI has taken all reasonable steps to locate further records sought by the applicant. In the circumstances, I find that CHI was not justified in refusing access to further records, under section 15(1)(a) of the FOI Act, on the grounds that no further records exist or can be found after all reasonable steps to ascertain their whereabouts have been taken.
While I am under no obligation to do so, I would strongly encourage the parties to engage with one another to determine the precise records the applicant believes ought to exist.
Decision
Having carried out a review under section 22(2) of the FOI Act, I hereby annul CHI’s decision. I find that CHI was not justified in refusing access to further records under section 15(1)(a) on the basis that further records do not exist or cannot be found after having taken all reasonable steps to ascertain the whereabouts of same and direct it to consider the matter afresh.
Right of Appeal
Section 24 of the FOI Act sets out detailed provisions for an appeal to the High Court by a party to a review, or any other person affected by the decision. In summary, such an appeal, normally on a point of law, must be initiated not later than four weeks after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.

Mary Connery
Investigator

title: Mr C & The Health Service Executive (the HSE)
text:
Decision
Mr C & The Health Service Executive (the HSE)
From
Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC)
Case number: OIC-161187-L6K1M5
Published on 9 July 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Right of Appeal
Whether the HSE was justified in its decision to refuse to confirm or deny, under section 37(6) of the FOI Act, the existence of records that mention the applicant
9 July 2026
Background
This review has its background in a previous decision this Office issued on 9 July 2025 in Case OIC-159213, wherein we annulled a decision of the HSE to refuse the applicant’s request under section 15(c) of the Act on the basis that it did not first properly comply with the provisions of section 15(4) of the FOI Act before doing so. We directed the HSE to process the request afresh.
The request was for all mentions of the applicant in any form (including variations of name and generic job title) by all staff in the hospital where he had worked as well as in his particular unit. He also specifically requested the same information from the accounts of 20 named individuals, including the CEO of the HSE. He requested all relevant records for the period 2 June 2023 to 12 February 2025.
On 22 July 2025, the HSE issued a fresh decision, wherein it refused the request under section 37(6)(b) of the Act. It said it considered that the disclosure of the existence or nonexistence of records may involve the disclosure of personal information relating to an individual or individuals other than the requestor which is prohibited under sections 37(1) and 37(7) of the FOI Act.
On 22 July 2025, the applicant sought an internal review of that decision. On 29 July 2025, the HSE issued its internal review decision wherein it affirm the original decision to refuse the request. On 5 August 2025, the applicant sought a review by this Office of that decision.
I have now completed my review in accordance with section 22(2) of the FOI Act. In carrying out my review, I have had regard to the correspondence outlined above, and to the correspondence between this Office and both parties on the matter. I have decided to conclude this review by way of a formal, binding decision.
Scope of Review
This review is concerned solely with whether the HSE was justified in its decision to refuse the applicant’s request for records that mention him under section 37(6) of the FOI Act.
Analysis and Findings
Section 37(1) of the FOI Act provides for the mandatory refusal of a request where the FOI body considers that granting access to the record sought would involve the disclosure of third-party personal information. Under section 37(6), where the FOI body considers that the disclosure of the existence or non-existence of the record sought would involve the disclosure of third-party personal information, it must refuse to grant the request and shall not disclose to the requester whether or not the record sought exists. Section 37(6) contains what is commonly referred to as a ‘neither confirm nor deny’ provision. It provides for the refusal of a request for access to a record and for the refusal to disclose whether or not such a record exists, provided the requirements of the subsection are met. The overall purpose of section 37(6) is to protect the personal information of a third party in situations where knowledge of the existence, or non-existence, of particular records would effectively disclose that party’s personal information. The usefulness of the provision depends upon it being invoked both in instances in which relevant records do not exist as well as in cases in which relevant records do exist.
Consideration of section 37(6) must be conducted on the basis of what would be the case were the FOI body to hold records of the kind sought by the requester, rather than on whether or not such records are actually held. For section 37(6) to apply, the following requirements must be satisfied:
• the record sought must be of a type which would disclose third-party personal information if it existed, and which would be exempt from release by virtue of section 37(1) of the FOI Act;
• none of the exceptions to the section 37(1) exemption, contained at subsections (2) or (5) of section 37, applies or, in the case where relevant records do not exist, would apply if such records did exist, and
• the FOI body must form the opinion that to state whether or not relevant records exist would, in itself, disclose third party personal information.
The question of whether confirming the existence or non-existence of relevant records would, in itself, disclose third party personal information generally depends on the nature of the records sought and on the manner in which the request has been framed.
In this case, the applicant essentially sought any records referencing him, either specifically, or by way of generic job title of the role he had held. I fully accept that it is possible that certain such records, if they exist, could contain third-party personal information. It is also possible that they could include nothing more than records created by the applicant’s colleagues in the course of the performance of their functions. On this point, I note that for the purposes of the FOI Act, where an individual holds or held a position as a member of the staff of an FOI Body, personal information does not include the name of the individual or information relating to the position or its functions or the terms upon and subject to which the individual occupies or occupied that position, or anything written or recorded in any form by the individual in the course of and for the purpose of the performance of his or her functions. Disclosure of the existence or non-existence of records coming within the scope of the request as framed in this case would disclose nothing more than the fact that the HSE either holds records that reference the applicant or it doesn’t. I fail to see how the disclosure of the existence or non-existence of such records, of itself, could possibly involve the disclosure of third-party personal information. If relevant records exist, disclosure of that fact discloses nothing about the contents of such records other than the fact that records exist that mention the applicant. Accordingly, I find that the HSE’s decision to refuse to confirm or deny the existence of relevant records pursuant to section 37(6) was not justified.
I would add, in any event, that by refusing the request in the first instance under section 15(1)(c) as it did in Case OIC-159213 (which provides for the refusal of a request where the FOI Body considers that granting the request would cause a substantial and unreasonable interference with or disruption of work of the FOI body concerned by reason of the number or nature of the records concerned), it seems to me that the HSE essentially indicated that it does, indeed, hold relevant records. This makes the HSE’s decision to rely on section 37(6) in its fresh consideration of the request rather strange.
As I have found that the HSE has not justified its decision to refuse to confirm or deny the existence of relevant records on the basis of section 37(6), and in order to preserve the HSE’s rights of appeal, I consider that I have no appropriate alternative other than to yet again remit the matter back to the HSE for consideration afresh.
The effect of this is that the HSE must, for a second time, consider the applicant’s request afresh and make a new, first instance decision in accordance with the provisions of the FOI Act. The applicant will have a right to internal review and a review by this Office if he is not satisfied with the HSE’s fresh decision. In the event that the applicant feels the need to apply to this Office for a further review, we will endeavour to prioritise any such review. I would also caution the HSE that pursuant to section 22(12)(b) of the FAOI Act, a decision to refuse to grant an FOI request is presumed not to have been justified unless the FOI body concerned can satisfy the Information Commissioner that its decision was justified. As such, if the matter appears before this Office again and the HSE fails to satisfactorily justify its decision, it runs a strong risk of records it considers exempt being released.
Decision
Having carried out a review under section 22(2) of the FOI Act, I hereby annul the HSE’s decision to refuse the applicant’s request under section37(6) of the FOI Act and I direct it to carry out a fresh decision-making process on the request.
Right of Appeal
Section 24 of the FOI Act sets out detailed provisions for an appeal to the High Court by a party to a review, or any other person affected by the decision. In summary, such an appeal, normally on a point of law, must be initiated not later than four weeks after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
Stephen Rafferty
Senior Investigator

title: Mr. Z & The Atlantic Technological University (ATU)
text:
Decision
Mr. Z & The Atlantic Technological University (ATU)
From
Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC)
Case number: OIC-200042-A0A0D2
Published on 8 July 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Preliminary Matters
Decision
Right of Appeal
Whether ATU was justified in its decision to refuse to disclose, under section 36(4) of the Act, whether or not records exist relating to the applicant's request
8 July 2026
Background
By way of background, ATU is a multi-campus technological university located in the west and northwest of Ireland.
On 11 November 2025, the applicant made a multi-part request to ATU for records relating to a staff request for additional resources to facilitate the provision of a specific educational course in conjunction with a third party.
On 10 December, ATU refused to either confirm or deny the existence of records under section 35(4) of the FOI Act.
On 11 December, the applicant requested an internal review of ATU’s decision.
On 22 December, ATU affirmed its original decision to neither confirm nor deny the existence of records. In its internal review decision, ATU did not reference any specific provision of the Act.
On 4 January 2026, the applicant applied to this Office for a review of ATU’s internal review decision. In his application, the applicant expressed dissatisfaction with the fact that ATU had refused to release any information.
During the course of the review, ATU confirmed that, rather than relying on section 35(4) as set out in its decision of 10 December 2025, it had intended to rely instead on section 36(4). The Investigating Officer informed the applicant of this material change in ATU’s position and offered him the opportunity to respond, which he duly did.
I have now completed my review in accordance with section 22(2) of the FOI Act. While I do not intend to repeat either ATU’s submissions or those of the applicant in full here, I can confirm that I have had regard to both for the purposes of this review. I have decided to conclude this review by way of a formal, binding decision.
Scope of Review
ATU has refused to either confirm or deny the existence of records coming within the scope of the applicant’s request, on the basis of section 36(4) of the FOI Act. This review is therefore solely concerned with whether ATU was justified in refusing the applicant’s request under section 36(4) of the Act.
Preliminary Matters
At the outset I wish to make some preliminary comments.
Firstly, it is important to note that while I am required by section 22(10) of the FOI Act to give reasons for my decisions, this is subject to the requirement of section 25(3) that, in the course of a review, I take all reasonable precautions to prevent disclosure of information that, if it were included in a record, would cause the record to be exempt from release. Accordingly, in the analysis which follows, I must be careful not to disclose whether or not records of the type sought by the applicant exist in light of ATU’s reliance on the relevant refusal to confirm or deny provision.
Secondly, in correspondence with this Office, the applicant said that he found it hard to believe that two different ATU decision makers had made the mistake of citing section 35(4) instead of section 36(4) when providing the reason for refusal of his request. The applicant questioned how the internal reviewer had made the same error as the initial decision maker despite the requirement for the former to carry out a fresh consideration of the request. While reminding the applicant that it is not within the remit of this Office to adjudicate on how FOI bodies perform their functions generally, or to act as an alternative dispute resolution mechanism with respect to actions taken by FOI bodies, I would also like to point out that the internal reviewer did not cite any provision at all when issuing the internal review decision.
Finally, the applicant asked whether ATU is entitled to change the provision upon which it is relying to refuse his request and queried whether there is any time limit that permits or denies this entitlement. As the Investigating Officer reminded the applicant, a review by this Office is considered to be ‘de novo’, which means that in this case, it is based on the circumstances and the law as they pertain at the time of the decision and is not confined to the basis on which the FOI body reached its decision.
Analysis and Findings
The FOI Act contains a number of what are commonly known as “neither confirm nor deny” provisions. The purpose of “neither confirm nor deny” provisions is to allow a public body to refuse to confirm or deny the existence of records sought where disclosure of the existence or non-existence of records could cause the types of harm envisaged by the relevant exemption provision. In deciding whether to avail of such provisions, the public body’s analysis may be carried out on a hypothetical basis, since the records may or may not in fact exist. Accordingly, there must be some additional factor – usually relating to the terms of the FOI request itself – which the public body can establish would give rise to the harm envisaged by the applicable exemption were it to confirm whether or not relevant records exist.
Section 36(4) contains one such provision. It requires an FOI body to refuse to confirm the existence or non-existence of records where it considers that disclosing the existence or non-existence of records would have an effect specified in section 36(1).
Section 36(1)(a) protects records containing trade secrets. Section 36(1)(b) provides for the mandatory refusal of a request if a record contains financial, commercial, scientific, or technical or other information the disclosure of which could reasonably be expected to result in a material financial loss or gain to the person to whom it relates or could prejudice the competitive position of that person. Finally, section 36(1)(c) protects records containing information the disclosure of which could prejudice the conduct or outcome of negotiations of the person to whom it relates.
For section 36(4) to apply, the following requirements must be satisfied:
(i) the records sought, if they existed, must be of a type that would be exempt from release by virtue of section 36(1) of the FOI Act;
(ii) none of the exceptions to the section 36(1) exemption, contained at sub-sections (2) or (3) of section 36, would apply, and
(iii) the FOI body must be of the view that to state whether or not relevant records exist would have an effect specified in section 36(1).
Having regard to the precise wording of the applicant’s request, it is reasonable to conclude that the disclosure of whether or not relevant records exist would be likely to disclose whether or not ATU had entered into an agreement, or was considering entering into an agreement, with the third party for the development and/provision of the specified college course. Having regard to the request made and the nature of the records sought, I am satisfied that to release the relevant records, if they exist, would involve the disclosure of information of a commercially sensitive nature. Although I am limited by the requirements of section 25(3) of the FOI Act in the extent to which I can discuss my reasoning, I consider that I am free to outline the basis for my view as follows. Given the wording of the request, I am of the view that the kinds of records sought by the applicant would, if they existed, be likely to contain financial or commercial information relating to ATU and/or a potential third party. I believe that it is therefore reasonable to conclude that release of such records, were they to exist, would be likely to prejudice the competitive position of an educational institution like ATU and/or the potential third party and/or prejudice the conduct or outcome of contractual or other negotiations.
Section 36 provides for certain circumstances where subsection (1) does not apply. Subsection (2) sets out certain circumstances in which the exemption at section 36(1) does not apply. I am satisfied that none of the circumstances provided for in subsection (2) would apply to the kind of information that would likely be contained in the requested records, if they existed. Subsection (3) provides that a request that would fall to be refused under section 36(1) may still be granted where the public interest would, on balance, be better served by granting than by refusing to grant the FOI request.
In considering where the balance of the public interest lies in this case, I have had regard to section 11(3) of the Act which provides that in performing any functions under the Act, an FOI body must have regard to, among other things, the need to achieve greater openness in the activities of FOI bodies and to promote adherence by them to the principles of transparency in government and public affairs and the need to strengthen the accountability and improve the quality of decision making of FOI bodies. In doing so, I have also had regard to the judgment of the Supreme Court in The Minister for Communications, Energy and Natural Resources and the Information Commissioner & Ors [2020] IESC 57 (“the eNet case”). In that case, the Supreme Court found that a general principle of openness does not suffice to direct release of records in the public interest and that “ there must be a sufficiently specific, cogent and fact-based reason to tip the balance in favour of disclosure
”.
In his initial submission to this Office, the applicant essentially argued that he considered it in the public interest for details of ATU expenditure to be made available to him. While this submission was made with respect to ATU’s then-reliance on section 35(4), I believe that this observation can be equally applied to section 36(4).
Section 36(1) is an express recognition of the fact that there is a public interest in the protection of commercially sensitive information. As a general principle, I do not believe that the FOI Act was designed as a means by which the commercial operations of organisations, even publicly funded ones, were to be opened up to scrutiny. The applicant has argued that the kinds of records he is requesting, if they exist, ought to be released in the interests of transparency. Although I acknowledge that there is a public benefit in ensuring transparency with regard to how a publicly funded educational institution like ATU spends its resources, this must be balanced against the right of such institutions to protect information of a commercially sensitive nature. In the circumstances, I am satisfied that, were records to exist, the public interest in granting the request would not, on balance, outweigh the public interest in protecting commercially sensitive information.
I therefore find that the records sought are of a type whose release, if they exist, would involve the disclosure of information of a commercially sensitive nature that would be exempt by virtue of section 36(1).
The final issue I must consider is whether the disclosure of whether or not relevant records exist would, of itself, disclose information of a commercially sensitive nature. While I believe I am restricted, by virtue of section 25(3), from explaining why, having regard to the wording of the applicant’s request and the nature of the records sought in this case, I accept that, in the specific circumstances of this case, the disclosure of the existence or non-existence of relevant records at this point in time would disclose information of a commercially sensitive nature within the meaning of section 36(1).
I find, therefore, that ATU was justified in refusing the request under section 36(4) of the FOI Act.
Decision
Having carried out a review under section 22(2) of the FOI Act, I hereby affirm ATU’s decision to refuse to disclose, under section 36(4) of the Act, whether or not records coming within the scope of the applicant’s request exist.
Right of Appeal
Section 24 of the FOI Act sets out detailed provisions for an appeal to the High Court by a party to a review, or any other person affected by the decision. In summary, such an appeal, normally on a point of law, must be initiated not later than four weeks after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
____________________
