title: Mr. X & TUSLA
text:
Decision
Mr. X & TUSLA
From
Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC)
Case number: OIC-160050-S7Q2N4
Published on 7 July 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Preliminary Matters
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Right of Appeal
Whether Tusla was justified in refusing access to records relating to a named deceased individual pursuant to section 37(1) and 37(8) of the Act
7 July 2026
Background
In a request dated 29 April 2025, the applicant sought access to all records held by Tusla (or its predecessor) relating to a named deceased individual. He said the request relates to any complaints, safeguarding concerns, case assessments, or institutional responses connected to the individual.
In a decision dated 29 May 2025, Tusla refused the request. It said the applicant’s request did not fall within the scope of section 37(8) of the FOI Act, which concerns Regulations that provide for the right of access to records of deceased persons by certain categories of individuals. The applicant sought an internal review of Tusla’s decision on 29 May 2025. In its internal review decision dated 19 June 2025, Tusla affirmed its refusal of the request on the ground that the records sought are exempt under section 37(1) of the Act. On 25 June 2025, the applicant applied to this Office for a review of Tusla’s decision.
I have now completed my review in accordance with section 22(2) of the FOI Act. In carrying out my review, I have had regard to the submissions made by both the applicant and Tusla. I have also had regard to the nature and contents of the records at issue. I have decided to conclude this review by way of a formal, binding decision.
Scope of Review
The scope of this review is concerned solely with whether Tusla was justified in refusing access, under section 37(1) of the FOI Act, to records relating to a named deceased individual.
Preliminary Matters
Before I address the substantive matters arising in this review, I wish to note that this Office has no remit to investigate complaints, to adjudicate on how FOI bodies perform their functions generally or to act as an alternative dispute resolution mechanism with respect to actions taken by FOI bodies. This review has been undertaken under section 22(2) of the Act and is confined to a consideration of whether the decision taken by Tusla on the applicant’s request was justified.
It is also important to note that while I am required by section 22(10) of the FOI Act to give reasons for my decision, section 25(3) provides that the Commissioner must take all reasonable precautions in the performance of his functions to prevent the disclosure of information contained in an exempt record or matter that, if it were included in a record, would cause the record to be an exempt record. Accordingly, the details I can provide of the information redacted in this case are somewhat limited, as are the reasons I can give for my decision.
Lastly, before I proceed to my analysis of the substantive matters relevant to this review, I wish to comment on the nature of the extensive submissions made by the applicant. He has referenced a number of legal authorities and conventions in support of his application. I have carefully considered these authorities and conventions in the context of whether Tusla has justified its decision to rely on the relevant FOI exemption provisions claimed in this case. I wish to observe that general references to legal authorities will often neither assist the applicant in making cogent submissions, nor assist this Office in assessing the submissions made by him. A number of assertions were made by the applicant which, once scrutinised, are not in fact supported by the authorities cited by him. In one such instance, the applicant’s submission refers to what is characterised as a previous decision of this Office which the applicant cited as ‘Mrs Y v Tusla (OIC-170275)’, which the applicant said is supportive of the position that “eligibility under the FOI Regulations is not strictly limited, and that survivors and litigants may obtain access in the public interest”. An investigator from this Office was unable to identify this case by reference to the case number and case name provided and indeed, the applicant was unable to locate a copy of same following a request from this Office. In any event, previous decisions of this Office do not necessarily have precedential value, and this Office must assess each case on its own merits and the factors to be considered as part of any public interest assessment on a case-by-case basis. Therefore, previous decisions of this Office will not necessarily be determinative of subsequent cases. Applicants who prepare submissions for this Office should ensure that their submissions are accurate and that they fairly reflect the authorities cited.
It is worth stating here that this Office has noted an increasing number of cases where submissions are being prepared with the assistance of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools. Our experience has shown that AI-generated correspondence can be inaccurate and can contain large volumes of material which is irrelevant in the context of the service we provide. Longer, AI-informed documents often lack the clear information we require in order to assess the issue involved. Instead, they often provide a substantial amount of additional information which does not help us deal with a case and, generally, these cases take longer to deal with.
Analysis and Findings
Section 37(1) & 37(7)
Section 37(1) of the FOI Act provides that, subject to the other provisions of the section, an FOI body shall refuse a request if access to the record concerned would involve the disclosure of personal information, including personal information relating to a deceased individual. This does not apply where the information involved relates to the requester (section 37(2)(a) refers). However, section 37(7) provides that, notwithstanding section 37(2)(a), an FOI body shall refuse to grant a request if access to the record concerned would, in addition to involving the disclosure of personal information relating to the requester, also involve the disclosure of personal information relating to an individual or individuals other than the requester (commonly known as joint personal information). Essentially, this means that while section 37(1) does not provide a basis for refusing access to personal information that relates solely to the requester, the request shall be refused pursuant to section 37(7) if that personal information is inextricably linked to personal information relating to parties other than the applicant.
Section 2 of the Act defines ‘personal information’ as information about an identifiable individual that, either (a) would, in the ordinary course of events, be known only to the individual or members of the family, or friends, of the individual, or (b) is held by the FOI body on the understanding that it would be treated by that body as confidential. Section 2 goes on to specify 14 categories of information which, without prejudice to the generality of the definition provided for under section 2, comprises personal information, these include (i) information relating to the educational, medical, psychiatric or psychological history of the individual, (vi) information relating to any criminal history of, or the commission or alleged commission of any offence by, the individual, and (xiv) the views or opinions of another person about the individual.
Having reviewed the records concerned, I am satisfied that they are records to which section 37(1) applies. I am not, unfortunately, in a position to provide a more detailed description of the information contained in the records in light of the requirement in section 25(3) of the Act that the Commissioner must take all reasonable precautions in the performance of his functions to prevent the disclosure of exempt information. Suffice to say, the records are of a highly sensitive and personal nature. Furthermore, having reviewed the records concerned, I am satisfied that the records to which section 37(7) applies are of a kind whereby the personal information of the applicant is inextricably linked to other individuals, and that section 37(7) applies to those records.
However, that is not the end of the matter, however, as section 37(1) is subject to the other provisions of section 37.
Section 37(2)
Section 37(2) of the FOI Act provides that section 37(1) does not apply if:
(a) subject to subsection (3), the information concerned relates to the requester concerned,
(b) any individual to whom the information relates consents, in writing or such other form as may be determined, to its disclosure to the requester,
(c) information of the same kind as that contained in the record in respect of individuals generally, or a class of individuals that is, having regard to all the circumstances, of significant size, is available to the general public,
(d) the information was given to the FOI body concerned by the individual to whom it relates and the individual was informed on behalf of the body, before its being so given, that the information belongs to a class of information that would or might be made available to the general public, or
(e) disclosure of the information is necessary in order to avoid a serious and imminent danger to the life or health of an individual,
In its submissions to this Office Tusla submitted that none of the provisions of section 37(2) apply to the records concerned. Having reviewed the records myself, some information contained in certain of the records contain information relating to the applicant. Save for those specific records, which I have considered in the context of section 37(7) above, I am satisfied that none of the provision of section 37(2) apply to the balance of the withheld records.
Section 37(5)
Section 37(5) provides that a request which would otherwise be refused under section 37(1) may be granted where on balance (a) the public interest that the request be granted outweighs the public interest that the right to privacy of the individual to whom the information relates should be upheld, or (b) the grant of the request would benefit the person to whom the information relates. I am satisfied that section 37(5)(b) does not apply in this case.
Before I consider the applicability of section 37(5)(a), there are a number of important points to note. First, section 13(4) provides that in deciding whether to grant or refuse an FOI request, any reason that the applicant gives for the request and any belief or opinion of the FOI body as to the reasons for the request shall be disregarded. In relation to the question of the public interest, this means that I cannot have regard to the applicant's motives for seeking access to the records at issue, except in so far as those motives reflect, or overlap with, what might be regarded as true public interest factors in favour of release of the records, i.e. insofar as the concerns raised in relation to the request may also be matters of general concern to the wider public.
Secondly, it is important to note when records are released under the FOI Act they are considered, in effect, to be released to the world at large, as the Act places no constraints on the uses to which a released record under the Act can be put. With certain limited exceptions provided for under the Act, FOI is not about granting access to information to particular individuals only and as noted above, an applicant's reasons for making a request are generally not of relevance. Thus, records are not released under FOI for any limited or restricted purpose.
All of this means that in considering whether a right of access exists to records under section 37(5)(a) of the Act, any decision to grant access would be on the basis that there is an overriding public interest in the release of the records effectively to the world at large that outweighs the privacy rights of the third party individuals concerned.
In considering where the balance of the public interest lies in this case, I have had regard to section 11(3) of the Act which provides that in performing any functions under the Act, an FOI body must have regard to, among other things, the need to achieve greater openness in the activities of FOI bodies and to promote adherence by them to the principles of transparency in government and public affairs and the need to strengthen the accountability and improve the quality of decision making of FOI bodies. However, in doing so, I have also had regard to the judgment of the Supreme Court in The Minister for Communications, Energy and Natural Resources and the Information Commissioner & Ors [2020] IESC 57. In that case, the Supreme Court found that a general principle of openness does not suffice to direct release of records in the public interest and “there must be a sufficiently specific, cogent and fact-based reason to tip the balance in favour of disclosure”. Although the Court’s comments were made in a case involving commercial sensitivity and confidentiality, I consider them to be relevant to the consideration of public interest tests generally.
In its internal review decision, Tusla said that it considered the following factors in favour of release of the records in question:
• The public interest in openness, transparency and accountability in the manner in which Tusla performs its functions.
• The public interest in members of the public knowing that the information held by public bodies about them, or those they represent is accurate.
• The public interest in members of the public exercising their rights under the FOI Act.
Tusla said it considered the following factors against release of the records sought:
• The public interest in protecting the right to privacy.
I accept that in this case, the applicant has made a complaint to Tusla concerning the named individual and that there is a public interest in the applicant being aware of how Tusla have handled his case and what (if any) investigations it has carried out on foot of same. Having had regard to the withheld records, it appears that the applicant has been made aware of what occurred in respect of his complaint and why Tusla ceased to have a role in any investigation.
In his submissions to this Office, the applicant made reference to a number of legal authorities including the Council of Europe Convention on the Protection of Children against Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse (“the Lanzarote Convention”), the Children First Act 2015. The applicant said these authorities support the proposition that the public interest favours the release of the records sought as he said that the records concern safeguarding transparency, systemic accountability, and the right to justice in abuse cases. The applicant has not cited any specific provisions of either authority, simply referring to them in a general way.
The applicant also made reference to jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights, namely its decisions in Gaskin v United Kingdom App no. 10454/83 (ECtHR, 7 July 1989) and O’Keeffe v Ireland App no. 35810/09 (ECtHR, 28 January 2014). The applicant said that these decisions were supportive of the proposition that there exists a right of access to ‘institutional records’ where child protection responsibilities were exercised and where such access is essential to legal redress. Following a review of these decisions, I am satisfied that these decisions do not create an unfettered right of access to records.
In any event, I have considered the content of the authorities cited by the applicant insofar as they could possibly relate to his entitlement to request access to records under FOI legislation. To that end, I find that the applicant’s submissions in that regard relate to the public interest in survivors of abuse being able to understand the steps taken by Tusla in handling and investigating their complaints.
Additionally, the applicant also said that there were a number of additional factors which favoured release of the records:
• He said that the High Court has already found special circumstances under section 27(4) of the Succession Act 1965, which led to the appointment of an independent administrator ad litem.
• He said that through an affidavit sworn by him, the Court is aware of multiple victims of the deceased individual and a pattern of abuse spanning a 20-year age gap.
• He said that Tusla records are directly relevant to establishing that pattern and to ensuring that the administration of the estate is conducted with full transparency in the context of live High Court proceedings.
These additional factors proffered by the applicant relate to the existence of High Court proceedings brought by him against the estate of the deceased. Those proceedings have not concluded, and I note that the appointment of an administrator ad litem to the deceased’s estate is “limited for the purposes of substantiating proceedings to be brought by the [applicant]”. The weight to be afforded to such factors when considering the public interest is, in my view, somewhat limited and personal in nature, since it is the applicant who has brought proceedings against the estate of the individual the subject of his request.
What remains to be considered, therefore, is information concerning third parties. The FOI Act recognises the public interest in the protection of the right to privacy both in the language of section 37 and the Long Title to the Act (which makes clear that the release of records under FOI must be consistent with the right to privacy). It is also worth noting that the right to privacy has a constitutional dimension, as one of the unenumerated personal rights under the Constitution. Moreover, unlike other public interest tests provided for in the FOI Act, there is a discretionary element to section 37(5)(a), which is a further indication of the very strong public interest in the right to privacy. Privacy rights will therefore be set aside only where the public interest served by granting the request (and breaching those rights) is sufficiently strong to outweigh the public interest in protecting privacy.
In light of the foregoing, I am satisfied that given the nature of the records at issue, which concern allegations of a most serious nature against the deceased individual, that there is even greater weight to be afforded to the right to privacy of third party individuals than would be the case in the ordinary course. The weight to be afforded to the right to privacy is already a significant one, and particularly so where release under FOI is, potentially at least, release to the world at large. I am not satisfied that there is a specific, cogent and fact-based reason which would outweigh the strong protection to be afforded to the right to privacy of any third parties in this case. I find, therefore, that section 37(5)(a) does not apply.
Section 37(8)
In his submissions to this Office, the applicant submitted that he is entitled to the records pursuant to section 37(8) of the Act. Section 37(8) of the Act provides that, notwithstanding subsection (1), the Minister for Public Expenditure and Reform may provide by regulations for the grant of an FOI request where the individual to whom the record concerned relates is dead and the requester concerned is a member of a class specified in the regulations.
The Freedom of Information Act 2014 (Section 37(8)) Regulations 2016 (S.I. No. 218 of 2016), as amended, are the relevant Regulations in this case (“the Regulations”). Amongst other things, the Regulations provide that, notwithstanding section 37(1) (and subject to the other provisions of the FOI Act), a request for records which involves the disclosure of personal information of a deceased individual shall be granted where the requester is a person on whom a function is conferred by law in relation to the individual or his or her estate acting in the course of the performance of the function.
In his submissions to this Office, the applicant said that he is such a person on whom a function is conferred by law in relation to the estate of the individual. To that end, the applicant submitted that he is the plaintiff in proceedings brought against the estate of the individual the subject of this request. In particular, the applicant cited the appointment of an administrator ad litem to the deceased’s estate by the High Court. The applicant provided a copy of the relevant Court order which identifies the administrator ad litem (who is a solicitor) and notes that the administrator ad litem’s appointment is “ limited for the purposes of substantiating proceedings to be brought by the [applicant
]”.
Tusla do not accept that the applicant belongs to a class of individual to whom section 37(8) and the Regulations apply. I should observe at this juncture that the appointment of an administrator ad litem to the estate occurred subsequent to the applicant’s application to this Office for a review. However, Tusla submitted that this development does not materially change matters.
The Regulations provide that a request for a record which involves the disclosure of personal information shall, subject to the other provisions of the Act, be granted where the individual to whom the record relates is dead and the requester is a person on whom a function is conferred by law in relation to the individual or his or her estate acting in the course of the performance of the function. Having considered the applicant’s submissions, I am satisfied that the applicant is not such an individual.
Prior to the appointment of the administrator ad litem, the applicant also said that his status as a complainant against the deceased individual and as a plaintiff in proceedings brought against the deceased’s estate conferred him with a function by law in respect of the deceased’s estate. I am satisfied that this could not possibly be the case. Quite apart from the fact that no “function” is conferred by law on the applicant, since it was he himself who made the complaint and initiated proceedings against the estate, if what the applicant contended was correct, any individual wishing to obtain sensitive records concerning a deceased individual need only initiate legal proceedings or make a complaint against that individual or his estate. I am satisfied that on no reading of the Regulations could this be the case.
Accordingly, in light of the foregoing, I have found that section 37(1) serves to exempt from release the records which the applicant seeks. The applicant has not demonstrated that he belongs to any category of individual set out in the Regulations and accordingly section 37(8) does not serve to disapply section 37(1).
Decision
Having carried out a review under section 22(2) of the FOI Act, I hereby affirm Tusla’s decision. I find that Tusla was justified in refusing access to the records sought pursuant to section 37(1).
Right of Appeal
Section 24 of the FOI Act sets out detailed provisions for an appeal to the High Court by a party to a review, or any other person affected by the decision. In summary, such an appeal, normally on a point of law, must be initiated not later than four weeks after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
Stephen Rafferty
Senior Investigator

title: Mr M & TUSLA
text:
Decision
Mr M & TUSLA
From
Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC)
Case number: OIC-162313-H0K6T3
Published on 7 July 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Preliminary Matters
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Right of Appeal
Whether Tusla was justified in refusing access to certain information in records relating to the applicant and his two sons on the basis of sections 31(1)(b), 37(1) and 37(7) of the FOI Act.
7 July 2026
Background
On 25 July 2025, the applicant submitted a request to Tusla for all records concerning him and his two sons from 23 January 2025 to date of the request.
Tusla issued its decision on 22 August 2025. The decision was accompanied by two schedules of records. The first schedule identified 99 records while the second identified 96 records. Tusla granted access to the records, with certain information redacted on the basis of sections 31(1)(b), 37(7) and 37(1) of the Act.
On 22 August 2025, the applicant requested an internal review on the grounds that there were numerous redactions which he thought was unreasonable. The applicant said that as the records concerned his children and he is their legal guardian, he was unable to see how certain redactions under section 37(1) of the Act could be applied to records referred to in both schedules. On 8 September 2025, Tusla affirmed the original decision, following which the applicant applied to this Office for a review of that decision.
I have now completed my review in accordance with section 22(2) of the FOI Act. In carrying out my review, I have had regard to the correspondence outlined above, and to the correspondence between this Office and both parties on the matter. I have also had regard to the contents of the records concerned. I have decided to conclude this review by way of a formal, binding decision.
Scope of Review
This review is solely concerned with whether Tusla was justified in redacting, under sections 31(1)(b), 37(7) and/or 37(1) of the Act, certain information from the records at issue.
Preliminary Matters
While I am required by section 22(10) of the FOI Act to give reasons for my decision, section 25(3) provides that the Commissioner must take all reasonable precautions in the performance of his functions to prevent the disclosure of information contained in an exempt record or matter that, if it were included in a record, would cause the record to be an exempt record. Accordingly, the details I can provide of the contents of the records at issue and of Tusla’s submissions in this case are somewhat limited, as are the reasons I can give for my decision.
I have noted the applicant’s contention that a number of false reports have been made about him and that such false reporting is a criminal offense under section 5 of the Protections for the Persons Reporting Child Abuse Act, 1998. Our role is confined to reviewing the decision taken by the FOI body concerning the applicant’s request for records however it is open to the applicant to take the matter of false reporting directly to An Garda Síochana.
It is also important to note that a review by this Office is considered to be “de novo”, which means that in this case, it is based on the circumstances and the law as they pertain at the time of the decision and is not confined to the basis upon which the FOI body reached its decision. Accordingly, in light of the “de novo” nature of our reviews, I consider it appropriate to consider the applicability of section 37(1) to all of the information at issue, notwithstanding the fact that Tusla relied on section 31(1)(b) as a ground for redacting some information from the records.
Analysis and Findings
Section 37
Section 37(1) of the FOI Act provides that, subject to the other provisions of the section, an FOI body shall refuse a request if access to the record concerned would involve the disclosure of personal information. This does not apply where the information involved relates to the requester (section 37(2)(a) refers). However, section 37(7) provides that, notwithstanding section 37(2)(a), an FOI body shall refuse to grant a request if access to the record concerned would, in addition to involving the disclosure of personal information relating to the requester, also involve the disclosure of personal information relating to an individual or individuals other than the requester (commonly known as joint personal information). Essentially, this means that while section 37(1) does not provide a basis for refusing access to personal information that relates solely to the requester, the request shall be refused if that personal information is inextricably linked to personal information is inextricably linked to personal information relating to parties other than the applicant.
Section 2 of the FOI Act defines personal information as information about an identifiable individual that, either (a) would, in the ordinary course of events, be known only to the individual or members of the family, or friends, of the individual, or (b) is held by an FOI body on the understanding that it would be treated by that body as confidential. The FOI Act details fourteen specific categories of information which is personal without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing definition.
The records at issue in this case comprise the social work files relating to the applicant’s two sons. The information to which access has been refused in the relevant records relates to names and details of third parties, information concerning third parties known to the applicant and joint personal information concerning the applicant and third parties. There are also records refused in part or in full which relate to Family Court proceedings. I note Tusla has also refused access to the names and the G numbers of Garda members.
In his submissions to this Office, the applicant said he is facing numerous false reports to Tusla and that the records he requested are heavily redacted to the point that the nature of the allegation is unclear. The applicant said that he has no issue with redaction of third party names or addresses but he did not see how the details of an allegation against him and specific words redacted in sentences could be exempt under section 37(1) of the Act.
In its submissions to this Office, Tusla said that the scope of the request involves two very similar files of the applicant’s children and the records concern a number of referrals which contain related arguments and allegations to Tusla. It said there are many instances of both personal and joint personal information held on file. It said there have been a number of ongoing Family Court proceedings. It said that certain information contained in the records belongs to sensitive categories of personal data and would therefore not be released to a third party. It said that where joint personal information could be separated and redactions applied to part of a sentence while still making sense to the reader upon release, redactions were carried out. Finally, Tusla said that it has closed the case from a child protection perspective as there was no direct harm to the children.
Having examined the records in both social work files, I am satisfied that all of the information withheld comprises either personal information relating to other third parties or joint personal information relating to the applicant and other third parties. In so far as the redacted information concerns the applicant and his children, I am satisfied that the release of such information would also involve the disclosure of personal information relating to third parties. I should say at this stage that the fact that the applicant may be aware of the nature of some or all of the information at issue does not mean that it cannot comprise personal information.
I also note the applicant’s contention that the redaction of certain words could not possibly fall for protection under section 37(1). He referenced, as an example, a word redacted that describes the nature of alleged abuse. I disagree. While I am constrained by the provisions of section 25(3) from providing a more detailed explanation, I am satisfied that section 37(1) applies to such information.
On the matter of the redaction of the names and identifying numbers of relevant members of An Garda Síochána (AGS), I note that the definition of personal information contained in the FOI Act excludes the names of staff members of FOI bodies. However, it is important to note that AGS is a partially included agency. Schedule 1 of the Act provides that AGS is an FOI body only insofar as it relates to administrative records relating to human resources, or finance or procurement matters. This Office takes the view that the name of a member of AGS, where it is contained in a record that is not a relevant administrative record, cannot be regarded as the name of a member of the staff of an FOI body, for FOI purposes. In this case, the names and G numbers of staff members of AGS are contained in reports prepared by AGS and Tusla in the context of operational duties. I am satisfied that these names and numbers should be treated as personal information and I find that section 37(1) of the Act applies.
I find, therefore, that section 37(1) applies to all of the information at issue. However, that is not the end of the matter as section 37(1) is subject to the other provisions of the section, specifically subsections (2) and (5). Accordingly, I must proceed to consider whether any of those other provisions serve to disapply section 37(1) in respect of any or all of the information at issue.
Section 37(2)
Section 37(2) provides that section 37(1) does not apply if;
a) the information concerned relates to the requester concerned,
b) the individual to whom the information relates consents, in writing or other such form as may be determined, to its disclosure to the requester,
c) information of the same kind as that available in the record in respect of individuals generally or a class of individuals that is, having regard to all the circumstances, of significant size, is available to the general public,
d) the information was given to the FOI body concerned by the individual to whom it relates and the individual was informed on behalf of the body, before it being so given, that the information belongs to a class of information that would or might be made available to the general public, or
e) disclosure of the information is necessary in order to avoid a serious and imminent danger to the life or health of an individual.
The purpose of section 37(2)(a) is to ensure that section 37(1) cannot apply to information relating solely to the requester. I am satisfied that the withheld information in the records that relates to the applicant is inextricably linked with personal information relating to third party individuals. I am satisfied, therefore, that section 37(2)(a) does not apply, pursuant to section 37(7). No argument has been made that any of the other circumstances outlined above at subsections (b) to (e) are relevant in this case, nor do I consider any to apply.
Section 37(5)
Section 37(5) provides that a request that would fall to be refused under section 37(1) may still be granted where, on balance (a) the public interest that the request should be granted outweighs the right to privacy of the individual to whom the information relates, or (b) the grant of the request would benefit the person to whom the information relates. No argument has been made that section 37(5)(b) applies in this case and I am satisfied that it does not apply.
Before I consider the applicability of section 37(5)(a), there are a number of important points to note. First, section 13(4) provides that, subject to the Act, in deciding whether to grant or refuse an FOI request, any reason that the requester gives for the request and any belief or opinion of the FOI body as to the reasons for the request shall be disregarded. In relation to the question of the public interest, this means that I cannot have regard to the applicant's motives for seeking access to the records at issue, except in so far as those motives reflect, or overlap with, what might be regarded as true public interest factors in favour of release of the records, i.e. insofar as the concerns raised in relation to the request may also be matters of general concern to the wider public.
Secondly, it is important to note that the release of records under the FOI Act must be regarded, in effect, as release to the world at large, given that the Act places no constraints on the uses to which a record released under the Act can be put. With certain limited exceptions provided for under the Act, such as under sections 37(2)(a) and 37(8), FOI is not about granting access to information to particular individuals only and as noted above, a requester's reasons for making a request are generally not of relevance. Thus, records are not released under FOI for any limited or restricted purpose.
All of this means that in considering whether a right of access exists to records under section 37(5)(a) of the Act, any decision to grant access would be on the basis that there is an overriding public interest in the release of the records effectively to the world at large that outweighs the privacy rights of the third-party individuals concerned.
In considering where the balance of the public interest lies in this case, I have had regard to section 11(3) of the Act which provides that in performing any functions under the Act, an FOI body must have regard to, among other things, the need to achieve greater openness in the activities of FOI bodies and to promote adherence by them to the principles of transparency in government and public affairs and the need to strengthen the accountability and improve the quality of decision making of FOI bodies. However, in doing so, I have also had regard to the judgment of the Supreme Court in The Minister for Communications, Energy and Natural Resources and the Information Commissioner & Ors [2020] IESC 57 (“the Enet case”). In that case, the Supreme Court found that a general principle of openness does not suffice to direct release of records in the public interest and “there must be a sufficiently specific, cogent and fact-based reason to tip the balance in favour of disclosure”. Although the Court’s comments were made in cases involving confidentiality and commercial sensitivity, I consider them to be relevant to the consideration of public interest tests generally.
In his submissions to this Office, the applicant contends that he is facing numerous reports made to Tusla and states he is unable to ascertain the nature of the allegations against him. He said the records are heavily redacted to the point that the nature of the allegations made is unclear.
The FOI Act recognises a public interest in ensuring the openness, transparency, and accountability of public bodies in how they perform their functions. I accept that there is a public interest in individuals against whom complaints are made to be afforded fair procedures and natural justice in the consideration by an FOI body of such complaints.
On the other hand, the FOI Act recognises the public interest in the protection of the right to privacy both in the language of section 37 and the Long Title to the Act (which makes clear that the release of records under FOI must be consistent with the right to privacy). It is also worth noting that the right to privacy has a constitutional dimension, as one of the unenumerated personal rights under the Constitution. Privacy rights will therefore be set aside only where the public interest served by granting the request (and breaching those rights) is sufficiently strong to outweigh the public interest in protecting privacy. Moreover, even where an overriding public interest in granting the request exists, there is a discretionary element to the application of section 37(5)(a).
In its submissions, Tusla said it considered the following factors in favour of release:
• the public interest in the public knowing how a public body performs its functions
• the public interest in members of the public knowing that information held by public bodies about them, or those they represent, is accurate
• the public interest in members of the public exercising their rights under the FOI Acts.
It considered the following factors against release:
• the public interest in protecting the right to privacy of members of the public
• the public interest in members of the public being able to communicate in confidence with public bodies and without fear of disclosure in relation to personal or sensitive matters
• the public interest in public bodies being able to perform their functions effectively.
It said that it considers the public interest in preserving the privacy of the third parties involved outweighs the public interest that would be served were the records to be released to the applicant. It said that the records are highly sensitive and release would have direct impact on a third party concerned and any potential future interactions with Tusla.
While the applicant has made no specific public interest arguments in respect of the records, it is very important to restate that the release of records under FOI must be regarded, potentially at least, as release to the world at large. As I have already outlined, any decision to grant access would be on the basis that there is an overriding public interest in the release of the records effectively to the world at large that outweighs the privacy rights of the third parties concerned.
Having considered the information already provided to the applicant, it seems to me that the public interest in enhancing the transparency and accountability of Tusla in relation to its handling of the relevant referrals has been met to a large extent by the release of a significant amount of the information at issue. In processing this FOI request, it seems to me that Tusla has endeavoured to release the records to the greatest extent possible whilst seeking to protect the privacy rights of third parties. Indeed, having regard to the level of information already released, it is not apparent to me that the applicant cannot ascertain the nature of the allegations against him or that they are unclear. The question I must consider is whether the public interest in ensuring the further transparency and accountability of Tusla by releasing the remaining information withheld outweighs, on balance, the public interest in protecting the privacy rights of the third parties concerned.
While some of the third party information contained in the records is not particularly sensitive in nature, it remains personal information, nonetheless. Moreover, much of the information is, indeed, particularly sensitive. Having considered the matter, and bearing in mind the strong public interest in protecting the right to privacy and the fact that release under FOI is, in essence, release to the world at large, I do not accept that the public interest in releasing the third party information outweighs, on balance, the privacy rights of the relevant third parties. I am not satisfied that any sufficiently specific, cogent and fact-based reason to tip the balance in favour of disclosure of this information exists in this case.
Accordingly, I find that section 37(5)(a) does not serve to disapply section 37(1) in respect of any of the information at issue. As I have found the records identified by Tusla, in both social work files, to be exempt under section 37, there is no need for me to go on to consider the applicability of section 31.
Decision
Having carried out a review under section 22(2) of the FOI Act, I hereby affirm the decision of Tusla to refuse access, in full or in part, to the records at issue under section 37(1) of the FOI Act.
Right of Appeal
Section 24 of the FOI Act sets out detailed provisions for an appeal to the High Court by a party to a review, or any other person affected by the decision. In summary, such an appeal, normally on a point of law, must be initiated not later than four weeks after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
Stephen Rafferty
Senior Investigator

title: Mr. Y & The Standards in Public Office Commission
text:
Decision
Mr. Y & The Standards in Public Office Commission
From
Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC)
Case number: OIC-200204-A0A0P6
Published on 6 July 2026
Background
Preliminary Matter
My Analysis
Decision
Right of Appeal
Whether SIPO was justified in refusing access to certain records relating to the applicant, under section 15(1)(a) of the Act, on the basis that relevant records do not exist or could not be found after it had taken all reasonable steps to identify and ascertain their whereabouts
6 July 2026
Background
On 3 December 2025, the applicant requested copies of any records held by SIPO that refer to him or to the release to him of documents relating to a named TD, which were the subject of a legal settlement between the TD and SIPO.
On 3 February 2026, as SIPO had not issued a decision within the statutory timeframe, the applicant requested an internal review of the deemed refusal.
On 10 February, SIPO informed the applicant that it had no record of his request having been made and asked him if he wished to proceed with the internal review or to avail of the opportunity to have an original decision made on his request. The applicant asked for the internal review to proceed.
On 3 March, SIPO refused the applicant’s request under section 15(1)(a) of the Act, saying that, following searches of folders and emails and consultation with relevant teams, its position was that no records exist that come within the scope of his request.
On 4 March, the applicant applied to this Office for a review of SIPO’s internal review request. In his application, he said that it was not tenable for SIPO to rely upon section 15(1)(a) as he is aware from an earlier similar request, made under GDPR, that records relating to the matter do exist. The applicant included a SIPO DSAR Schedule from 2024, which, according to him, is evidence of the existence of relevant records. He said that he believes that some of these records contain commentary about him and his work as a journalist.
I have now completed my review in accordance with section 22(2) of the FOI Act. During the course of this review, the Investigating Officer requested submissions from SIPO. While I do not intend to repeat in full either SIPO’s submissions or those made by the applicant at the time of his application, I can confirm that I have had regard to both for the purposes of this review. I have decided to conclude this review by way of a formal, binding decision.
Scope of Review
SIPO has refused the applicant’s request under section 15(1)(a) of the Act. As such, this review is concerned solely with whether SIPO was justified in refusing access to records relevant to the applicant’s request on the basis that no relevant records exist or can be found after all reasonable steps have been taken to ascertain their whereabouts.
Preliminary Matter
Before I address the substantive issues arising, I wish to make a preliminary comment.
It is important to note that a review by this Office is considered to be “de novo", which means that in this case, it is based on the circumstances and the law as they pertain at the time of the decision and is not confined to the basis upon which the FOI body reached its decision.
Analysis and Findings
Section 15(1)(a)
Section 15(1)(a) of the FOI Act provides for the refusal of a request where the records sought do not exist or cannot be found after all reasonable steps to ascertain their whereabouts have been taken. Our role in a case such as this is to review the decision of the FOI body and to decide whether that decision was justified. This means that I must have regard to the evidence available to the decision maker and the reasoning used by the decision maker in arriving at their decision and also must assess the adequacy of the searches conducted by the FOI body in looking for relevant records. The evidence in “search” cases generally consists of the steps actually taken to search for the records along with miscellaneous and other information about the record management practices of the FOI body, insofar as those practices relate to the records in question.
SIPO’s submissions
In its submissions to this Office, SIPO outlined the searches it had conducted for records relevant to the applicant’s request.
At the outset, it said that all electronic records held by SIPO, including records relating to FOI requests, were maintained on its Document Management System (DMS), which was its primary archive. However, it said that further to a cyber-attack on 11 December 2025 this DMS was no longer available to it and as such it was not possible for any searches to be carried out of this repository for records relevant to the applicant’s request. However, SIPO said that some residual folders, with incomplete records, were identified on its G:Drive.
SIPO said that, on 10 February 2025, the decision maker had asked the applicant to identify any FOI requests he had previously made relating to the TD as this would facilitate searches for records relevant to his current request. However, SIPO said that the applicant had declined to do so.
SIPO further said that the decision maker consulted with the Head of the SIPO Secretariat and the Head of the Complaints and Investigations Unit (CIU) to ascertain where on SIPO’s remaining drives any potential records relevant to the applicant’s request would most likely be found. It said that following such consultation it was determined that any possible records would be found among FOI records. In the absence of a DMS to search, the view was that any records would exist only in the residual and incomplete FOI folders on the SIPO G:Drive.
SIPO said that it first searched the incomplete FOI folders only for records linking the applicant to the TD, i.e. not for records that relate to the applicant alone. However, SIPO said that it subsequently searched the folders for records relating to the applicant. It said that all folders that were located subsequent to these searches were examined and have been saved in the 2026/05 folder. SIPO said that it also searched for records relating to the TD but that there were no results.
SIPO further said that, as the decision maker was aware that there were more FOI requests from the applicant than these searches had identified, he proceeded to examine the full FOI log and all FOIs submitted by the applicant in order to find any between 2021 and 2025 that concerned the TD, bearing in mind that the legal matter referred to by the applicant occurred in 2021/2022. SIPO provided details of these search results by year. For the years 2023 to 2025, the decision maker searched all notes in the FOI logs, which it said contained nothing concerning the applicant and the TD combined. For the year 2022, as there were no notes on the log, SIPO said the decision maker searched in each folder pertaining to the applicant, but this resulted in nothing being found that concerned both the TD and the applicant combined. Finally, SIPO said that, for the year 2021, there were no notes in the FOI log and that a search of all existing folders showed that there were none relating to the applicant. According to SIPO, the decision maker also searched any FOI records on his H: Drive that referred to the applicant to see if any pertained to the TD, but there were none. SIPO said that from these searches it appeared that no records pertaining to the TD and the applicant existed and that a refusal on administrative grounds was the only option available. SIPO said that it had concluded that any further records relating to an FOI request by the applicant with respect to the relevant TD were now no longer available.
In addition, SIPO noted the applicant’s reference to the DSAR folder in his application to this Office. It said that this information would have been very useful at the time of the original request but that it was not provided. SIPO said that, in the absence of a cross-referenced DMS archive, there is no effective way to locate records other than to find folders where relevant records might exist and then to examine the content of these folders. SIPO said that, with this new information, CIU was able to find a DSAR folder on the SIPO G:Drive. SIPO said that, in this folder, it located a number of records connected to the applicant, including records relating to a previous FOI request, an email chain between the applicant and a SIPO staff member in which the applicant made enquiries and received answers, and two copies of a newspaper article on the TD written by the applicant. SIPO noted that the applicant will already be in possession of these records. According to SIPO, neither a DSAR decision letter nor a DSAR schedule of records were found in the DSAR folder.
SIPO went on to say that its normal practice was to retain FOI files on the DMS. SIPO also said that the applicant may be correct in saying that relevant records existed in 2024 but added that all DSAR requests and records were held on the DMS, which is no longer accessible and cannot be searched.
The Investigating Officer subsequently shared the DSAR schedule with SIPO, with a view to assisting more targeted searches. SIPO noted that the DSAR schedule details six released records and 45 legal advice records that were not released. SIPO said that it had compared the schedule with the contents of the G:Drive folder. According to SIPO, there is no similar grouping of records in the G:Drive folder but it acknowledged that there may have been a folder on the DMS containing the records. SIPO went on to say that it considered it most likely that the six released records listed on the schedule were those that it found on its G:Drive. With respect to the 45 legal advice records listed in the DSAR schedule, SIPO noted that the G:Drive folder contains a very large number of legal advice records. SIPO reiterated that it searched this folder and all sub-folders but could find no records that contain commentary about the applicant and his work as a journalist as referenced in the title of the record. SIPO said that the 45 legal advice records may have been compiled in a separate folder on the DMS. SIPO concluded that, in order to see if there may be a reference to the applicant in any of the legal advice records (the titles of which do not refer to him), however tenuous that possibility, it would be necessary to read through all the records in the DSAR folder.
The Investigating Officer subsequently sought further information from SIPO with respect to the records and the searches carried out. In its response, SIPO explained that the applicant’s relationship to the case of the TD was peripheral at best and it surmised that the legal advice records mentioned in its submission may have been included in the applicant’s DSAR folder purely because his newspaper article and the email chain were there.
SIPO went on to say that there were a total of 150 legal advice records relating to the case in a folder labelled ‘SIPO Legal Advice Library [TD’s initials]” and that these relate entirely to the legal process. SIPO explained that this was in addition to 102 records located in the other folders. SIPO said that it had searched the folders and examined all the titles of each of the records, reiterating that the only references to the applicant were as it had already detailed. SIPO added that, if it is necessary to search within each record using a keyword search, then this could be done but that it would take some time. SIPO reiterated that the records on the G: Drive are, at best, residual and incomplete and that this applies to the DSAR request records and the schedule that were prepared by the Data Protection Officer (DPO) at the time.
Finally, the SIPO decision maker said that he had discussed the matter with the current DPO and requested that she search for a possible DSAR folder on the G: Drive containing records that would respond to the DSAR Schedule. The decision maker added that, although such a folder is likely to have been saved on the DMS as the primary archive, there may be a residual folder that would help with this search process.
My Analysis
It is important to note that the FOI Act does not require absolute certainty as to the existence or location of records, as situations can arise where records are lost or simply cannot be found. What the FOI Act requires is that the public body concerned takes all reasonable steps to locate relevant records.
The question I must consider, therefore, is whether SIPO has taken all reasonable steps to ascertain the whereabouts of the specific records sought.
At the outset, I note that it is clear that further to the cyberattack of 11 December 2025, SIPO no longer has access to its primary electronic archive; the DMS. While this is unfortunate, it means that any searches for records relevant to the applicant’s request will necessarily be confined to what is termed the G:Drive which is acknowledged by SIPO to be residual and incomplete.
In the circumstances of the case, I am satisfied that the key issue which I must consider is whether SIPO has conducted all reasonable searches of the G:Drive for records relevant to the applicant’s request.
Having regard to the information before this Office, I am not satisfied that SIPO has taken all reasonable steps to locate the records sought by the applicant. It is evident from SIPO’s submissions that its searches to-date have located relevant records and, while it maintains that these are in the applicant’s possession, it does not appear to have verified this with the applicant. In addition, while I appreciate that searches have been complicated by the loss of the DMS and that the repository of records on the G: Drive appears to be residual and incomplete, SIPO’s submissions indicate that further searches could be conducted with a view to confirming whether relevant records still exist. While SIPO has indicated that these searches may take some time, I do not believe that the number of records involved would make such searches unreasonable.
Accordingly, having regard to the information before this Office, I simply cannot find that SIPO has taken all reasonable steps to locate further records sought by the applicant. In the circumstances, I find that SIPO was therefore not justified in refusing access to further records, under section 15(1)(a) of the FOI Act, on the grounds that no further records exist or can be found after all reasonable steps to ascertain their whereabouts have been taken.
Decision
Having carried out a review under section 22(2) of the FOI Act, I hereby annul SIPO’s decision. I find that SIPO was not justified in refusing access under section 15(1)(a) of the FOI Act to further relevant records coming within the scope of the applicant’s request and I direct it to make a fresh decision on the applicant’s FOI request.
Right of Appeal
Section 24 of the FOI Act sets out detailed provisions for an appeal to the High Court by a party to a review, or any other person affected by the decision. In summary, such an appeal, normally on a point of law, must be initiated not later than four weeks after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.

Investigator

title: Ms. Y & The Health Service Executive
text:
Decision
Ms. Y & The Health Service Executive
From
Office of the Information Commissioner (OIC)
Case number: OIC-200165-A0A0M3
Published on 6 July 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Preliminary Matters
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Right of Appeal
Whether the HSE was justified in refusing the applicant’s request for safeguarding records relating to her son on the basis that the records do not exist or cannot be found after it had taken all reasonable steps to identify and ascertain their whereabouts
6 July 2026
Background
By way of background to this case, the HSE provides long-term homecare services to the applicant’s son via a private company that acts as a service provider to the HSE. Although the applicant’s son made the original request with the support of his mother, his mother represented him from internal review stage onwards, including the application to, and interactions, with this Office. As such, all references to “ the applicant
” in this decision are references to the mother of the original requester.
On 6 May 2025, the applicant’s son made a request to the HSE for all information (electronic and otherwise), emails, reports and outcomes/results regarding safeguarding reports made by the relevant home care provider relating to him. He said that there were a number of reports starting in late 2023/early 2024 and during 2024. He also sought the same information relating to a report made by his mother on his behalf on around 18 December 2024.
On 2 October 2025, the HSE part-granted the applicant’s son’s request, releasing nine HSE records. The HSE withheld information from some of these records under section 37(1) of the FOI Act, which it said was personal information of third parties. The HSE confirmed that it had requested and obtained the applicant’s consent under section 37(2) for release of personal information relating to her but that it had neither sought nor obtained the consent of the other third parties concerned.
On 29 October, the applicant requested an internal review of the HSE’s decision, and made specific reference to what she considered to be missing records.
On 18 December, the HSE varied its original decision, releasing further records that it said it had obtained from the home care provider. The HSE labelled the home care provider records ‘File B’, while the originally released HSE safeguarding records were labelled ‘File A’. The interal reviewer affirmed the decision to refuse access to certain information in File A on the basis of section 37(1) and also withheld certain information from the File B records on the same basis.
On 16 February 2026, the applicant applied to this Office for a review of the HSE’s internal review decision. In her application, she specifically maintained that the HSE had refused to release a safeguarding plan related to a safeguarding complaint made by her in December 2024.
In the course of the review by this Office, the applicant confirmed that she was not contesting the redactions made by the HSE in the released records.
I have now completed my review in accordance with section 22(2) of the FOI Act. During the course of this review, the Investigating Officer provided the applicant with details of the HSE’s submissions and offered her an opportunity to respond, which she duly did. While I do not intend to repeat either the HSE’s submissions or those of the applicant in full here, I can confirm that I have had regard to both for the purposes of this review. I have decided to conclude this review by way of a formal, binding decision.
Scope of Review
As set out above, in the course of correspondence with this Office, the applicant indicated that she was not contesting the redactions made to the relevant records on the basis of section 37(1). In the circumstances, I am satisfied that I do not need to consider this further as part of my review.
In addition, in her application to this Office, the applicant said that the HSE was refusing to release a specified safeguarding report with respect to her son. However, in the course of the review by this Office, the HSE told the Investigating Officer that the safeguarding report referred to by the applicant does not exist. This means that the HSE is effectively refusing access to the report on the basis of section 15(1)(a) of the Act which provides for the refusal of a request where the records sought do not exist or cannot be found.
Therefore, this Office’s review is solely concerned with whether the HSE was justified in refusing the applicant’s request under section 15(1)(a) of the Act.
Preliminary Matters
At the outset I wish to make some preliminary comments.
Firstly, this Office has no remit to investigate complaints, or to adjudicate on how FOI bodies perform their functions generally, or to act as an alternative dispute resolution mechanism with respect to actions taken by FOI bodies. Our role is confined to reviewing the decision taken by the FOI body on the applicant’s request for records.
Secondly, this Office’s review is solely concerned with the 2014 FOI Act and it is not within this Office’s remit to consider the GDPR.
Analysis and Findings
Section 15(1)(a)
Section 15(1)(a) of the Act provides for the refusal of a request where the records sought do not exist or cannot be found after all reasonable steps to ascertain their whereabouts have been taken. The role of this Office in a case such as this is to review the decision of the FOI body and to decide whether that decision was justified. This means that I must have regard to the evidence available to the decision maker and the reasoning used by the decision maker in arriving at their decision and also must assess the adequacy of the searches conducted by the FOI body in looking for relevant records.
The evidence in “search” cases generally consists of the steps actually taken to search for the records along with miscellaneous and other information about the record management practices of the FOI body, insofar as those practices relate to the records in question. It is also important to note that the FOI Act is concerned with access to records that a public body holds as opposed to records that a requester considers ought to exist.
As noted above, the HSE provided this Office with information on the searches that it undertook to locate relevant records, details of which were provided to the applicant. The applicant also made submissions in support of her view that further records ought to exist. While I do not propose to repeat the submissions from both parties in full here, I confirm that I have had regard to them for the purposes of this review.
The parties’ submissions
In its submissions to this Office, the HSE confirmed that the home care provider is a service provider funded by the HSE for the provision of services to the applicant’s son. According to the HSE, the home care provider has confirmed that a meeting took place with the carer in relation to the alleged incident at the time of the applicant’s complaint in December 2024 and that the carer provided a statement. The HSE also said that the home care provider deemed that the matter was not a safeguarding one and that it did not log a safeguarding report.
The HSE also confirmed that the home care provider is satisfied that it provided the HSE’s internal reviewer with all records in its possession relating to safeguarding referrals relevant to this request. The HSE said that the home care provider has confirmed that it has no safeguarding records in relation to a report made by the applicant on 18 December 2024. The HSE also said that it is satisfied that it holds no further records in relation to preliminary screening or safeguarding records from the home care provider following receipt of the applicant’s formal safeguarding complaint in December 2024. The HSE said that the Acting Principal Social Worker has confirmed that the service has not received any further records.
The HSE provided details on the searches that both it and the home care provider carried out to find relevant records. According to the HSE, both its Disability Services and its Safeguarding Service records were searched. In the Disability Services, the Service User Chart and the Service User Home Support Chart were searched, while in the Safeguarding Service, the Online System for Adult Safeguarding (OSAS) was searched. The HSE said that Disability Services are satisfied that no records exist in relation to this matter and are satisfied that records are not misfiled. The HSE said that all safeguarding records are managed under OSAS, filed under the service provider name and service user name. The HSE said that the OSAS search was completed using both the service provider and service user name.
According to the HSE, the home care provider searched its One Touch System as well as all emails and service user documentation. The HSE said that keywords used in searches included the name of the service user, the name of the applicant, the name of the service provider, the name of the Ward of Court (i.e. the applicant’s son) and the word “incident”. The HSE also listed the names of HSE staff members (Disability Services and Safeguarding Services sections), as well as staff members of the home care provider, who were consulted.
The HSE added that both it and the home care provider are satisfied that the records sought do not exist.
In her application to this Office, the applicant said that, following the alleged December 2024 incident she had unsuccessfully attempted to obtain a safeguarding report from the HSE or a follow-up with the home care provider. She referred to a number of documents, including her complaint letter to the HSE of December 2024 and a letter from a HSE Social Worker following a telephone conversation she had with the latter. The applicant also referred to a HSE telephone note of 29 April 2025 (page 29 in File A) in which the HSE Social Worker made a record of a call she had with a representative of the home care provider regarding the alleged incident. The applicant noted that, according to this record, the HSE Social Worker informed the home care provider representative that the HSE Safeguarding and Protection Team (SPT) cannot provide the information relating to the alleged incident and that the SPT only provides oversight of same.
The applicant also highlighted that the note recorded the home care provider’s representative as saying that he would seek authorisation to have the safeguarding plan given to the applicant and the Social Worker as stressing the importance of ongoing communication with the applicant as her son’s guardian, to which the home care provider’s representative agreed. In further communication with this Office, the applicant said that she had been recently told by the home care provider that it would commence an investigation into the alleged incident. She also said that the home care provider confirmed that, as per its area safeguarding log for recording all safeguarding matters in line with HSE Safeguarding Vulnerable Adults policy, no safeguarding concern or communication had been received from the HSE in relation to the incident.
As outlined above, the Investigating Officer shared details of the HSE’s submissions with the applicant, who submitted her own observations in which she continued to maintain that, despite the HSE’s submissions, the evidence points to the existence of a safeguarding report concerning the safeguarding complaint made by her on 18 December 2024. She said that the HSE phone note dated 29 April 2025 records a definite discussion about an existing safeguarding plan. The applicant attached a response from the HSE “Your Service, Your Say” (YSYS) service dated June 2026. She said that the YSYS response observes that, according to the April 2025 phone note, the HSE Safeguarding Team advised the home care provider that she was requesting a copy of the safeguarding plan and that the home care provider is recorded in the same phone note as having stated that it will seek authorisation to have the safeguarding plan given to the applicant as requested. According to the applicant, this information states that a safeguarding plan was made but she said that it was not shared or discussed with her or her son. The applicant maintained that the document clearly exists but that the home care provider has not provided same to her.
The applicant also said that, although the home care provider has told her that no safeguarding referral was made to the HSE about the incident in question, she made three reports - one to the clinical care manager, one to the Home Care Manager and copied to local Disability Services Manager, in addition to reporting to the HSE Safeguarding Team. She also said that it is quite extraordinary that the home care provider deemed that the matter was not one when she had reported it to the home care provider and had made a safeguarding complaint herself. She said that the home care provider claims that the incident did not meet the threshold for a safeguarding complaint but that the other documents prove this to be incorrect.
My Analysis
It is important to note that the FOI Act does not require absolute certainty as to the existence or location of records, as situations can arise where records are lost or simply cannot be found. What the FOI Act requires is that the public body concerned takes all reasonable steps to locate relevant records. Furthermore, it is open to this Office to find that an FOI body has satisfied the requirements of section 15(1)(a), even where records that an applicant believes ought to exist, or are known to have existed in the past, have not been located. We do not generally expect FOI bodies to carry out extensive or indefinite general searches for records simply because an applicant asserts that records sought ought to exist or did exist.
The question I must consider, therefore, is whether the HSE has taken all reasonable steps to ascertain the whereabouts of the specific records sought.
Both the HSE and the home care provider maintain that they hold no safeguarding records relating to the complaint made by the applicant in December 2024. The applicant maintains that such records ought to exist.
I accept that the applicant reported the alleged incident both to the HSE and to the home care provider in December 2024. I also accept that the HSE Social Worker phone note of 29 April 2025 indicates that the HSE requested that the home care provider carry out a preliminary screening in relation to the alleged incident and that a subsequent safeguarding plan be put in place and shared with the applicant. However, according to the HSE’s submissions, the home care provider deemed that the matter was not a safeguarding one and therefore did not log a safeguarding report. In essence, both the HSE and the home care provider affirm that safeguarding records do not exist because they were never created. Having carefully considered the wording of the April 2025 phone note, I am satisfied that, despite the applicant’s assertion, there is no mention of an already existing safeguarding plan, only a request from the HSE that the home care provider develop one and share it with the applicant when completed.
I fully appreciate the applicant’s frustration that, despite raising her complaint in December 2024, she is not satisfied that the matter has reached a satisfactory conclusion. I also accept that the HSE phone note of April 2025 appears to give the impression that, at the very least, a preliminary screening form was to have been completed by the home care provider in respect of the alleged incident. However, the purpose of this Office’s review in cases like this is not to decide what records ought to exit or what records ought to have been created but to decide whether or not the FOI body has carried out all reasonable searches to locate records.
Having carefully considered the HSE’s submissions in this matter, I am satisfied that it has provided a sufficiently detailed and cogent explanation as to why no further records exist other than those which have been released to the applicant. Whilst I acknowledge the applicant’s arguments that further records ought to exist and I also acknowledge that the HSE appears to have requested the creation of preliminary screening records and a safeguarding plan, in the absence of any evidence to suggest that further searches are warranted in this case, I am satisfied that the HSE and the home care provider have carried out all reasonable steps to search for and provide the relevant records which are within the scope of the applicant’s request.
Accordingly, I find that the HSE was justified in refusing access to further records within the scope of the request under section 15(1)(a) of the Act on the basis that the records do not exist or cannot be found after all reasonable steps to ascertain their whereabouts have been taken.
Decision
Having carried out a review under section 22(2) of the FOI Act, I hereby affirm the HSE’s decision. I find that the HSE was justified in refusing access to safeguarding records relating to the applicant’s December 2024 complaint on the basis of section 15(1)(a) of the Act.
Right of Appeal
Section 24 of the FOI Act sets out detailed provisions for an appeal to the High Court by a party to a review, or any other person affected by the decision. In summary, such an appeal, normally on a point of law, must be initiated not later than four weeks after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
